units.title: How to think and learn as a payments advisor
units.objective: Connect commercial objectives, payment mechanics, risk ownership and technical evidence.

blocks.v: This programme prepares banking subject-matter experts to advise on payments with commercial judgement and architectural depth. Your objective is to explain how a service works, who bears its risks and what evidence supports a proposed change. Credibility comes from those connections and precise boundaries, rather than the number of acronyms used.

v: Start with the customer outcome: who pays whom, in which currency, by when and with what protection?
Identify the business model: revenue, balances, customer ownership and loss allocation.
Choose the instrument, scheme, access and settlement arrangement.
Define liquidity, exception handling and operational accountability.
Assign data and decision authority, then design consistency and recovery.
Support the recommendation with a scoped source, calculation or representative test.

units.objective: Use precise vocabulary without treating informal labels as legal categories.

head: Layer
Meaning
Example
rows: Means or agreed procedure for paying

Credit transfer, direct debit, card. Note the legal term differs: under PSD2 a payment instrument is the personalised device or procedure, while credit transfers and direct debits are payment services.

blocks.v: A rail is shorthand for a payment network, system or route; clarify its components. One scheme can use several infrastructures, and a company can both manage rules and operate processing.

v: Account-to-account (A2A) describes account endpoints. It can be standard, instant, domestic, international or on-us; it need not involve a PISP.
Instant/real-time describes a service promise of rapid funds availability, commonly continuously available; the named scheme defines timing and finality.
RTGS means real-time gross settlement: instructions settle individually without amount netting. It does not itself imply retail access or 24/7 operation.
RTP is also the proper name of The Clearing House’s US network. Request to Pay is a separate concept.

blocks.v: For a euro instant transfer, the customer uses a credit transfer under SCT Inst rules, cleared through a CSM such as RT1 or settled directly in TIPS. EPC manages the scheme; EBA CLEARING operates RT1; the Eurosystem operates TIPS. RT1 and TIPS are not alternatives at the same layer. RT1 is a clearing mechanism that settles in central-bank money in TIPS — either across the participant's own TIPS dedicated cash account or across EBA CLEARING's ancillary-system technical account. Choosing RT1 does not avoid TIPS; it changes which account the bank's position actually sits in, and therefore who funds it and when. That is the question to ask.

blocks.title: Executive application
blocks.v: When a supplier says “we support instant”, ask which currencies, participants, limits, protections and exception flows are supported. Turn the label into an assessable service.

units.title: Clearing, settlement and finality
units.objective: Distinguish information exchange, discharge of obligations, availability and later redress.

blocks.v: Clearing exchanges/processes instructions and, where applicable, calculates obligations. Settlement discharges obligations using the agreed asset. Some infrastructures integrate these functions closely.

head: Concept
Question
Consequence
rows: Funding is needed when released; queues can arise.
Liquidity savings require management of pre-settlement exposure/default.
When is settlement legally unconditional and irrevocable?
When may the beneficiary use funds?
Can a later duty move money back?
Does not make original final settlement provisional.

blocks.v: If A owes B €100 and B owes A €90, gross settlement processes both full amounts; bilateral netting produces a €10 obligation from A to B. Real systems add multilateral netting, queues and liquidity-saving mechanisms.

A customer deposit is a bank liability; a bank’s central-bank balance is a different claim. Central-bank settlement reduces settlement-asset credit exposure but does not remove fraud, legal, liquidity or operational risks.
An SDD Core refund right or card chargeback can create a subsequent obligation after final settlement. Avoid describing finality as the absence of customer protection.

units.title: Card payments: authorisation, clearing, settlement and disputes
units.objective: Understand card economics and mechanics before comparing cards with account payments.

v: The merchant/gateway sends an authorisation through acquiring/processing and network arrangements to the issuer.
The issuer applies controls and approves or declines; approval may create a hold.
Capture presents the financial transaction for clearing; amount/timing rules depend on the use case.
Network settlement discharges institutional obligations under its rules.
The acquirer/provider pays the merchant according to its contract, reserves and schedule.
Refunds and disputes are subsequent workflows with evidence and financial consequences.

blocks.v: Issuer serves the cardholder; acquirer serves the merchant. A gateway supplies connectivity and a processor performs processing functions; one provider may combine them. A four-party model separates cardholder, issuer, merchant and acquirer, with the network connecting them. Other arrangements combine roles.

Authorisation is not settlement and settlement is not necessarily merchant payout. Hotels, incremental authorisations, partial captures and recurring payments illustrate why a single success flag is inadequate.

head: Economic component
Meaning
rows: Fee between card-side institutions under network arrangements, typically acquiring to issuing side.
Charges for scheme and processing services.
Part of the merchant’s acceptance price.

blocks.v: EU caps apply to scoped card categories, not the merchant’s entire price. US Regulation II governs certain debit interchange and routing, with exemptions. Neither “all cards capped” nor “all US interchange uncapped” is accurate. Tokenisation reduces credential exposure without removing all fraud or PCI DSS obligations.

blocks.title: Executive application

units.title: Settlement mechanisms, timing and liquidity efficiency
units.objective: Compare gross, net and continuous arrangements without conflating them with customer speed.

head: Arrangement
Mechanism
Risk/liquidity question
rows: Who covers exposure before settlement and a participant default?
How are funds, queues and intraday credit managed?
Release individual orders under system funding rules
What enables release and establishes finality?
Rapid availability under a defined service
How does its actual interbank settlement work?

blocks.v: STEP2’s current design uses continuous gross settlement during its operating arrangements; do not describe it with its old deferred-net model. CHIPS combines liquidity-saving/netting mechanisms with continuous intraday finality, rather than simply settling everything at day end. Different fast systems use materially different settlement designs, and this is the most commonly botched fact in the domain. RT1 and TIPS settle each euro instant payment in central-bank money as it happens. UK Faster Payments is not RTGS: the customer gets funds in seconds, but participants' net obligations settle three times each business day in the Bank of England's RTGS, against balances they have prefunded in collateral accounts sized to cap their maximum possible net debit. Bacs settles once per business day on the same prefunded basis. Only CHAPS settles gross in real time. Customer speed and settlement design are independent — say so before anyone assumes otherwise.
Prefunding — the settlement fact of the instant era

A deferred net system carries exposure between settlement cycles: if a participant fails before the cycle runs, the others are owed money that was never funded. Prefunding removes that exposure by capping it in advance. Participants hold funds in a dedicated account — a TIPS dedicated cash account, an RT1 position, a Bank of England prefunding or collateral account — equal to the maximum net obligation they are allowed to reach. The cap is the control; the account is the evidence. Once you see this, three things follow that an advisor should be able to state without notes.

v: Liquidity moves from end-of-day to always-on. A netted batch world funds itself once a day against known positions. An instant world funds itself continuously against unknown ones, which is why weekend and holiday funding became a treasury problem rather than an operations one.

The cap is a business limit, not a technical one. Hitting it stops payments even though the platform is healthy. Capacity planning for instant payments has a funding axis as well as a throughput axis.

Intraday central-bank credit is generally unavailable out of hours. T2 is closed at the weekend while TIPS keeps running, so the prefunded position has to carry the institution until the RTGS reopens.

A profitable institution can still fail a payment because funds sit in the wrong settlement account at the required moment. That is a liquidity-placement failure, not a solvency one, and it is the failure mode executives most often miss.

blocks.v: Named systems, so this is not abstract. Deferred net, prefunded: UK Faster Payments (three settlement cycles a business day), Bacs (one), US ACH through FedACH and EPN, and card-network settlement. Real-time gross: CHAPS, T2, Fedwire Funds. Continuous gross with liquidity coordination: STEP2-T, CHIPS. Settled individually in central-bank money as they occur: TIPS, and RT1 positions settling in TIPS.
The settlement-risk vocabulary you will be tested on

head: Risk
What it is
How it is addressed
rows: One side delivers and the other fails before delivering back — the classic cross-currency FX case, named after the 1974 Bankhaus Herstatt failure
Payment-versus-payment settlement, principally through CLS; a material share of global FX turnover still settles without it
Exposure to a participant that fails before a deferred net cycle settles
Prefunding, net debit caps, collateral, loss-sharing arrangements
Funds are owed and owned but not in the right account at the right time
Intraday credit, liquidity-saving mechanisms, queue management, treasury placement
A failed participant's transactions are removed and every other participant's net position is recalculated
Prefunding and finality rules that make settlement legally unconditional so unwind cannot happen
A completed settlement is challenged by an insolvency administrator
Designation under the Settlement Finality Directive in the EU and UK; UCC Article 4A and Regulation J for US wires

blocks.title: Finality has a legal basis, not just a technical one
blocks.v: "When is this final?" is a question about law and system rules, not about when a message arrived. In the EU and UK, designated systems are protected under the Settlement Finality Directive: the moment of entry and the moment of irrevocability are defined in the system's own rules, and settlement then survives a participant's insolvency. In the US, UCC Article 4A governs wholesale credit transfers and Regulation J governs Fedwire. If someone tells you a payment is final, the follow-up is: final under which system's rules, and designated where?

Gross need not mean every instruction consumes fresh liquidity independently: incoming funds, queuing and coordinated release can save liquidity. Netting reduces required settlement amounts but creates obligations and default arrangements that must be understood.

blocks.title: Illustrative liquidity case
blocks.v: Weekend outflows total €12m and inflows €10m. Their €2m difference is not a sufficient funding estimate for a gross instant service if most outflows arrive first. Model the time profile, available funding and stress buffer.
Legal finality attaches to the specified system event. Distinguish it from availability, reversals permitted before settlement and later refund/return obligations.

blocks.title: Executive application
blocks.v: Ask how the service releases payments and funds peak obligations. Total daily net flow can conceal the liquidity required to keep a continuous promise.

See also — the market-by-market detail of who operates which system, and how each settles, is in module 03. The liquidity consequences of these designs return in unit 08.1 as a capacity question with a funding axis.

units.title: Direct debit, recurring transfers and Request to Pay
units.objective: Distinguish collection authority from a request message and from payment execution.

head: Method
Who starts value movement?
Authority and rights
rows: Payer-defined recurring transfer; different protection model.
Amount/time/scope limits and applicable service terms.
The request alone moves no money
Payer responds and, if agreed, a separate payment executes.

blocks.v: SDD Core and SDD B2B are different SEPA direct-debit schemes. Core includes an eight-week unconditional refund right for authorised collections; unauthorised-transaction claims have separate rules. B2B is for eligible business payers and has no corresponding refund right for an authorised collection; mandate verification and exceptions remain important. The numbers are worth stating rather than deferring. SDD Core: an 8-week unconditional refund right from the debit date for an authorised collection, and 13 months for an unauthorised one. SDD B2B: no refund right for an authorised collection, and the debtor bank must verify the mandate. Those asymmetries, not the message format, are why the two schemes have different customer populations. Confirm the current rulebook version before implementation.

SEPA Request-to-Pay (SRTP) carries a request and response, not settlement. Correlate request, invoice, payer response and payment ID; acceptance of a request is not proof of paid funds. OCT Inst is a separate credit-transfer scheme for a qualifying one-leg-out euro payment.

blocks.title: Worked collection

units.title: SCT Inst and FedNow: clocks, deadlines and uncertainty
units.objective: Budget processing against the correct scheme clock and handle timeout evidence safely.

blocks.v: A legal deadline, scheme processing timer, operator timeout and customer SLA are different measures. Define their start and end events before comparing numbers.

head: Service
Clock and response
Design consequence
rows: The current EPC rules work within the 10-second legal customer deadline and use 5/7/9-second subtimings.
Budget validation, risk, posting, network and persistence; follow the precise timestamp definition.
The readiness guide describes a 20-second clock from message creation, with a limited receiver response interval of 1–5 seconds.

blocks.v: The 2025 SCT Inst rulebook sets four boundaries, and they are obligations on named actors rather than targets. 5 seconds — the Originator PSP must have received either the message that the funds have been made available or a rejection. 7 seconds — the hard Time-Out Deadline: the Beneficiary PSP's CSM must by then hold the Beneficiary PSP's positive or negative confirmation, failing which the CSM generates a negative confirmation itself. 9 seconds — that confirmation must have reached the Originator PSP. 10 seconds — the legal deadline in the amended SEPA Regulation, which obliges the payee's PSP to make the amount available on the payee's account within ten seconds of the payer's PSP's time of receipt. Note whose clock starts when: the legal clock runs from the payer PSP's receipt of the payment order, not from the customer's tap. If no confirmation arrives in time, the Originator PSP must immediately lift the reservation and restore the payer's account — that is a prescribed remedy, not evidence that the external transfer never happened. Handle late confirmation and customer notification explicitly.

For FedNow, follow the current Operating Procedures for acceptance, rejection, status enquiries and reconciliation. The explanatory guide recommends status enquiry after the relevant waiting interval; do not treat a missing response as authority for a fresh duplicate payment.

ACWP (Accept Without Posting), described in the September 2025 procedures, applies to specified legal/compliance concerns about beneficiary availability. Settlement occurs while posting/availability may be delayed under defined follow-up duties. It is not an escape hatch for ordinary core latency. Consult the current procedure before implementing this exceptional path.

The historical FedNow PDF is retained as a study reference, explicitly dated. Use the current service page to identify superseding rules. SCT Inst no longer has the former scheme-level €100,000 cap; institution/customer limits still need assessment.

blocks.v: This is the single most commonly botched fact in UK payments, including by people who work in it. "Faster Payments is real-time gross" is wrong, and correcting it politely is a cheap and durable credibility marker. Note also that the Bank of England has admitted non-bank payment service providers to RTGS settlement accounts since 2018 and offers omnibus accounts — a materially more open access model than the US, where the Federal Reserve does not generally grant master accounts to non-banks.

SEPA geography is not identical to the EU, the European Economic Area (EEA) or the euro area. Currency, participation and regulatory scope must be checked independently. The Eurosystem comprises the ECB and euro-area national central banks.

Under the Instant Payments Regulation this is no longer a commercial choice on the euro leg: euro-area PSPs had to be reachable to receive from 9 January 2025 and able to send from 9 October 2025, with non-euro-area and non-bank PSPs following through 2027. The remaining decision is how — direct participation or a sponsored arrangement — not whether. Reachability, funding, technical connectivity and customer availability are separate requirements, and an interface to one service does not guarantee every endpoint.

blocks.v: OUR, SHA and BEN indicate payer-borne, shared and beneficiary-borne charge arrangements where permitted. They do not override a scheme’s own charge rules or guarantee an exact received amount without a supporting service commitment.

Business effect
Possible response

Funding design, extended availability or suitable interlinking.

blocks.v: Interlinking fast systems, OCT Inst and digital-money routes address particular frictions rather than the whole problem. Evaluate live coverage and both legs' rules before claiming a corridor works. And state the G20 targets precisely, because the two sets are routinely confused: retail cross-border payments — global average cost at or below 1%, with no corridor above 3%, by end-2027; remittances — global average cost of sending $200 at or below 3%, with no corridor above 5%, by 2030; and for speed, 75% of payments in each segment credited within one hour, the remainder within one business day, by end-2027. Against that, the World Bank's most recent published figure is a global average of 6.36% on $200 (Q3 2025), and the provider spread is wider than the regional spread — banks average close to 15% while digital-only money transfer operators average under 4%. The cost problem is channel and operating model before it is geography. A target is not evidence the market has achieved it, and the FSB's own progress reporting says the targets are unlikely to be met.
What actually changed in correspondent banking

v: Swift gpi added an end-to-end service layer over correspondent banking: a UETR preserved unaltered along the chain, a tracker giving status at each hop, a same-day availability commitment, fee transparency, and unaltered remittance data. It did not change the settlement model — it made it observable. That distinction is the answer to "what has actually improved since 2017?"
Pre-validation checks beneficiary account details and the target jurisdiction's payment rules before the payment is sent. Its value is a network effect: coverage, not capability, is the constraint.

The ISO 20022 cutover happened. MT/MX coexistence for cross-border payments and reporting ended on 22 November 2025 — MT 103 and MT 202 are gone for this traffic. MT 199/299 survive for gpi tracking, and the cancellation and investigation messages survive until the Case Management mandate in November 2027.

Project Nexus moved from blueprint to institution: the central banks of India, Indonesia, Malaysia, the Philippines, Singapore and Thailand established Nexus Global Payments as a legal entity in 2025, with the BIS stepping back from operator to adviser. It is not live.

What did not change is the liquidity model. Interlinking two domestic instant systems does not solve last-mile funding: somebody still has to hold a balance in the destination currency, and that cost reappears as an FX spread.

blocks.title: Payment-versus-payment, and the risk that is still there
blocks.v: The FX leg of a cross-border payment carries principal risk — you pay away one currency and rely on receiving the other. CLS addresses it by settling both legs simultaneously, payment-versus-payment, for eligible currencies and participants. A material share of global FX turnover still settles without PvP protection, which is why this is a live supervisory topic rather than a solved one. If a corridor design does not say how the FX leg settles, it has not addressed its largest risk.

blocks.v: Ask where the customer’s time and money are consumed. Recommend the intervention that removes the actual friction, rather than assuming a new network solves every corridor.

blocks.v: Know the three pricing shapes, because a merchant conversation turns on them. Interchange-plus (IC++) passes interchange and scheme fees through at cost with a stated margin — transparent, and the mix risk sits with the merchant. Blended quotes one rate for everything — simple, and the mix risk sits with the acquirer, who prices for it. Standard tiered pricing sorts transactions into qualification buckets and is the least transparent. When a merchant says card acceptance costs 1.4%, the useful question is which of the three they are quoting and what their card mix is.

blocks.title: The account-to-account counterfactual, done properly
blocks.v: A2A's pitch is a flat fee against an ad valorem cap, which means the business case is a function of average basket size and nothing else. Against a 0.2% debit cap, a flat fee of 8p breaks even at a £40 basket: below that cards are cheaper, above it A2A is. That is why pay-by-bank wins first in tax, utilities, financial services and high-value deposits, and why it has made almost no progress in everyday retail. Any A2A strategy that has not segmented by ticket size is wrong on the arithmetic before it starts.

Instant execution compresses float and moves the liquidity requirement from end-of-day net funding to continuously prefunded positions — a TIPS dedicated cash account, a prefunded collateral account, a liquidity management transfer. The effect on net interest income is not that balances disappear; it is that they turn over faster and must be held where they can settle, which raises the cost of carrying liquidity while reducing settlement-risk exposure. Whether the institution loses income depends on whether balances leave it or merely move faster inside it — and that is an answerable question, not a rhetorical one. The IPR prohibits a PSP charging more for an instant euro credit transfer than for a corresponding non-instant one — it does not cap a premium, it removes the ability to charge one. It does not regulate every adjacent commercial service. The consequence for a business case is blunt: there is almost never an incremental-revenue story for instant payments on the euro leg, so the case has to be built on cost, retention or the cost of non-compliance.

Define cost per successful, reconciled payment as relevant platform, network, people, controls, exception and funding costs divided by the specified completed population. Report attempted volume and losses alongside it; distinguish marginal from allocated costs.

blocks.title: Illustrative case

Total cost of ownership (TCO) includes dual running, licences, resilience capacity, data retention, network traffic and exit. Avoid double-counting fewer cases and faster case handling. Stress volume, adoption, fraud and delivery assumptions.

blocks.v: For euro-area credit institutions, the receive obligation applied from 9 January 2025 and the send obligation from 9 October 2025. Verification of Payee went live on the same date, 9 October 2025 — it is a separate obligation that happens to share the deadline, and it applies to standard credit transfers as well as instant ones. Non-euro-area credit institutions follow in January and July 2027, with Verification of Payee for them on 9 July 2027; payment institutions and e-money institutions have their own dates, including April 2027, and there is a further derogation into 2028 for out-of-hours national-currency cases. Note the legal category that drives all of this: the regulation distinguishes credit institutions from payment institutions and e-money institutions, which is precisely why "bank" is not a usable shorthand here. Use the official matrix for scope and special cases rather than applying one date to every institution.
Confirmation of Payee is not Verification of Payee

EU Verification of Payee

Phased from 2020, with wider coverage mandated later

Match / close match / no match / verification not possible

blocks.v: These two are the most commonly conflated pair in the domain. They solve the same problem under different law, on different rails, with different result vocabularies. Knowing which one someone means — and saying so — is a fast way to establish that you work in this rather than read about it.
What the IPR actually did to sanctions screening

This is where regulation meets architecture, and it is the strongest story in this module. Screening every instant payment against sanctions lists inside a ten-second window does not work: the list lookup is fast, but the hit review is human and is not. So the regulation changed the control point. PSPs verify their own customers against EU targeted financial restrictive measures at least once every calendar day, and immediately after any new designation enters into force, instead of screening each instant payment between euro-area PSPs. The control moved from the transaction to the customer base.

v: What this creates is a data pipeline, not a screening engine. You need list ingestion, delta detection against the previous version, a re-screen of the affected customer population, and an auditable record that it ran — every day, and within hours of a new designation.

It does not remove per-payment screening everywhere. Parties who are not your customers — the beneficiary, intermediaries, free-text remittance content — and the entire cross-border Swift flow still require message-level screening. The relief is specific to the euro-area instant leg.

The false-positive rate is now a commercial variable, not a compliance detail. Fuzzy-match tuning determines analyst headcount, and analyst headcount determines whether the product is viable. Ask for alerts per thousand payments and minutes per case, not for the match algorithm.

Decide in advance what happens when a hit fires inside the window. The payment cannot wait for a human. Either it rejects with a defined reason and the customer is told, or the institution accepts a control it cannot operate at speed. There is no third option, and the answer belongs in the design, not in the runbook.

blocks.v: Verification of Payee sits before authorisation, outside the ten-second execution clock — a point experts routinely get wrong in both directions. It is a pre-authorisation round trip to a directory, and its latency is the customer's waiting time, not the scheme's.

VoP can return match, close match, no match or unavailable/other defined results. It supports a customer decision; it does not prove the beneficiary is honest or eliminate scams. Handle joint/business names, aliases, data quality, service unavailability and customer warnings under the applicable rules. The requirement covers relevant standard as well as instant credit transfers.

The IPR’s targeted financial restrictive-measures provisions require screening of customers at least daily and on relevant changes. They do not abolish AML, fraud controls or every sanctions obligation. Distinguish the specific legal scope from a generic statement that instant payments cannot be screened.

blocks.v: Authorised Push Payment (APP) fraud deceives the customer into sending money. Account takeover uses compromised access. Merchant disputes and non-delivery present other questions. These cases have different prevention, evidence and redress paths.

Combine account history, device/session signals, beneficiary risk, behaviour, velocity and payment context within appropriate permissions and latency. An alert is not a conviction; escalation, review and appeal/complaint handling matter. Measure fraud loss, prevented loss, false declines, completion and case effort together.

Liability and reimbursement depend on jurisdiction, customer, instrument and circumstances, and irrevocable settlement does not extinguish later reimbursement duties. The UK regime is the most developed example and you should be able to state it: mandatory reimbursement of authorised push payment scam victims went live on 7 October 2024, covering UK-to-UK payments over Faster Payments and CHAPS, with a maximum of £85,000 per claim, the cost split 50:50 between the sending and receiving institution, reimbursement within five business days, an optional excess of up to £100, and vulnerable customers exempt from the excess and the claim-handling standards that would otherwise apply. Two things to carry: the 50:50 split is what forced receiving-side controls into existence, because for the first time the bank receiving a mule payment pays for it; and the regime's supervisory ownership is moving, since the Payment Systems Regulator is being consolidated into the Financial Conduct Authority, with the reimbursement requirements transferring across. head: Requirement
Define
Measure
rows: p50, p95, p99 and missed deadlines.
Recovery point/data-loss objective for a failure
Which acknowledged work survives the tested event.
Recovery time for the defined service
Restored outcomes, not just restarted processes.
Ability to change, detect and recover

blocks.v: Availability, in minutes rather than nines

head: Objective
Permitted unavailability per year
Per 30 days
What that means at 500 payments/second
rows: Roughly 1.3 million failed payments a year
Roughly 13,000 — and a single five-minute peak-hour outage exhausts the whole year

blocks.v: Two disciplines follow from that table. First, a percentage is not a commitment until you state the denominator — which customer action, which population, which dependencies, and which failures count as eligible attempts. "The platform was up" is not the same claim as "eligible payments completed". Second, nines are the wrong unit under a ten-second deadline: a scheme does not care about your annual percentage, it cares whether this payment met its clock. Report missed deadlines alongside availability, or the number flatters you.

blocks.title: Error budgets — the mechanism that makes an objective operational
blocks.v: An error budget is simply 1 minus the objective, expressed as permitted failure in a period, and spent by both incidents and changes. At 99.99% you have 4 minutes 20 seconds a month. A risky release that costs you 90 seconds of it is a legitimate decision; three of them is not. The point is that it converts an argument about whether to ship into an arithmetic question with an agreed answer, and it gives operations and delivery the same number to manage. If the budget is exhausted, change stops until it recovers. State the budget, the burn rate and the trigger, or the service objective is decoration.

Keep three terms apart, because executives blur them. An SLI is the measurement (the ratio of successful eligible attempts). An SLO is the internal target for that measurement. An SLA is a contractual commitment with a remedy attached, and it should always be looser than the SLO — if you promise externally what you are targeting internally, you have no margin to manage.

A “zero RPO” target needs a specified failure model, acknowledgement policy and topology. Majority acknowledgement is not a promise against every correlated disaster. Active-active applications do not automatically mean multi-primary writes or safe ownership of the same payment.

Model peaks, skew, payloads, risk calls, ledger posting, reporting and maintenance. A happy-path average can hide tail latency and a failing dependency. Capacity should include resilience headroom, not just the point at which a test saturates.

Test dependency failure, process loss, replica election, network partition, resource saturation and safe upgrades. Record customer/accounting outcomes and replay behaviour alongside recovery speed.

units.title: Integrity, consistency and idempotency
units.objective: Design one economic effect and resolve uncertainty across system boundaries.

blocks.v: ACID describes Atomicity, Consistency, Isolation and Durability for a defined database transaction. It does not atomically include another bank’s settlement. Establish invariants: permitted state transitions, one economic effect per logical operation, balanced postings and controlled available-funds changes.

v: Assign a stable logical-operation key and scope (for example tenant and operation).
Enforce uniqueness and compare the request fingerprint; reject incompatible reuse.
Atomically record the key, valid state/version transition and local effect or publication intent.
Return the recorded result/state on replay; define retention and in-flight behaviour.
For external attempts, retain durable transmission identity and resolve unknown outcomes through supported status/reconciliation before resubmitting.

blocks.v: An increment is not idempotent — applying it twice changes the balance twice. What you can make effectively-once is the handler: when the unique operation identity and the increment commit inside one atomic boundary, the second delivery is suppressed before the increment is applied. Say it that way, because a distributed-systems engineer will hear "idempotent increment" as a category error. Merely replacing an increment with a set is not a general solution either: stale writes then overwrite valid changes. Use conditional version updates, transactions, or carefully designed single-document atomic operations.

head: Delivery semantic
What it guarantees
Where it applies
rows: Never delivered twice; may be lost
Never lost; may be delivered many times
What every durable broker and retrying client actually gives you
Nothing, across a network boundary — it is not achievable in the general case
A claim to challenge whenever a vendor makes it
The effect is applied once, because the consumer records the message identity atomically with its effect
The property you actually design for

blocks.v: The reason exactly-once delivery is unachievable is worth being able to say in one sentence: the sender cannot distinguish a lost request from a lost acknowledgement, so it must either retry (risking duplication) or not (risking loss). Every real system chooses at-least-once delivery and then makes the effect idempotent. And the payments-specific corollary: exactly-once message handling does not establish exactly one completed economic payment — the message layer and the money are different systems, and reconciliation is what joins them.

What it provides
Boundary
rows: Timeout does not prove the write did not occur.
Consistent point-in-time view in supported use
Not a free default for every query.

blocks.v: Fence stale workers after ownership changes. Persist outbox/inbox identities with effects. Handle transaction retries and unknown commit results according to the driver/database contract. units.objective: Choose distribution around workload, authority and failure domains.

blocks.v: Sharding distributes data across partitions to scale capacity. Replication maintains copies for durability and availability. In a sharded MongoDB deployment the shards and the config servers are replica sets; the routers are stateless processes you run several of — a distinction worth getting right, because it determines what fails over and what you simply restart. Adding shards does not remove shared bottlenecks.

head: Key property
Payment consequence
rows: Too few distinct values limit distribution.
A dominant tenant/account can create a hot shard.
An increasing leading value can concentrate new writes.
Missing relevant key fields may cause scatter-gather.

blocks.v: A tenant-only key can overload a large tenant. A tenant plus suitably distributed payment identity can spread its work but changes targeting and account-level coordination. Hashed keys can distribute inserts; hashed indexes cannot themselves be unique. In sharded collections, enforce supported unique indexes with the shard-key prefix; do not assume _id is globally enforced when it is not the shard key.

One high-contention account or shared limit can still serialize work. Increasing partition count does not multiply its write authority. Measure read/write mix, indexes, working set, network, cross-shard transactions and dependency limits before extrapolating linear scale.

Zone placement supports controlled data location but does not automatically establish regulatory residency. Review replica placement, backups, logs, search copies and access. Cross-region writes trade latency against resilience and require a clear failure model.

units.title: Read the Icon/MongoDB benchmark critically
units.objective: Use measured evidence without expanding its scope into a production guarantee.

blocks.v: The public Icon Solutions summary dated 8 September 2026 reports scaling from 500 to 6,000 payments/second, mean end-to-end latency of 0.51 seconds at 6,000, approximately 430,000 database operations/second and persistence under 30 milliseconds. Its application-node failure exercise was run at 3,500 payments/second — 58% of peak, and the benchmark therefore contains no evidence about node loss at 6,000; throughput returned to that stable rate in about 90 seconds with zero data loss. Database primary election averaged about five seconds, within a single cloud region across three availability zones — which says nothing about regional loss or cross-region recovery point, and those are exactly the questions a resilience conversation is actually about. These are observations from described tests, not universal service commitments.

head: Question
Why it matters
rows: What constitutes a payment and end-to-end latency?
External risk, core and scheme boundaries may differ from the client’s service.
Payload, indexes, history and read/write mix determine cost.
Regions, replicas, concerns and failure assumptions affect guarantees.
Mean latency hides deadline misses and headroom.
A failure result cannot automatically be extrapolated to every peak/disaster.
No lost request is not by itself proof of correct economic effects.
Capacity matters alongside economics and maintainability.

blocks.v: The topology is published, so use it rather than deflecting: 12 application pods with integrated streaming, a 5-shard cluster for the event journal and a 6-shard cluster for the operational data store, on M80-class shards of 32 vCPUs and 128 GB, deployed in one cloud region across three availability zones. What is genuinely unreported is the part that determines whether the numbers transfer: write and read concern, the index set, payload shape and size, streaming partitioning, and which integrations the harness stood in for. Ask for those, and reproduce a representative workload before extrapolating. "I cannot speak to the topology" is the wrong answer to a question any attendee can look up.

blocks.title: The ratio that answers the unit's own question
blocks.v: The roughly 430,000 database operations per second split into about 236,000 on the event journal and 196,000 on the operational data store. At 6,000 payments per second that is about 72 database operations per payment. That single ratio is the whole lesson in reading a benchmark: database operations are not payments, the multiplier is a property of the design — event sourcing plus a separate read model — and quoting the larger number as though it were throughput is the most common way these figures get misused. It also tells you what to ask about any competing figure: operations per payment, and what the design is doing with them.

One more condition worth carrying: persistence latency roughly halved between database versions at a fixed rate in the same test series. That is a useful datum and a warning — a benchmark result is bound to a software version as much as to a topology, so a number quoted without its version is not a number.

Keep payment TPS distinct from database operations. Explain near-linear scale as a measured range under the tested workload, not a law that every extra shard doubles capacity. Use the benchmark to formulate a proof exercise tied to business outcomes.

blocks.v: Present a qualified observation, then the test needed for the client. This is stronger evidence than converting a vendor result into an unconditional architecture promise.

See also — the service objectives this benchmark is evidence for are defined in unit 08.1. A throughput number without an availability objective, a latency percentile and a stated failure model is a marketing figure, not an engineering one.

units.title: Stablecoins: claims, reserves and payment economics
units.objective: Evaluate the whole payment service, including redemption and legal rights.

blocks.v: A stablecoin is a crypto-asset designed to track a reference value; stability is an objective, not a guarantee. Ask who owes the holder what, who may redeem and what happens in insolvency. Token transfer, discharge of an invoice and bank-account payout are different events.

head: Design
Stability mechanism
Risk question
rows: Asset quality, custody, access and run liquidity.
Correlated price falls, congestion and liquidation failure.
What sustains the peg when confidence disappears?
A bank claim represented as a token
Different liability/rights; not automatically a stablecoin.

blocks.v: Trace acquisition, control checks, network transfer, custody, redemption/FX and local payout. Include conversion spread, network fees, funding, compliance, support and exit. Cheap on-chain transfer is only one cost component; recipient usable funds are the relevant outcome.

MiCA distinguishes e-money tokens (EMTs), referencing one official currency, from asset-referenced tokens (ARTs) referencing other values or combinations; classification determines obligations. Two date corrections worth carrying, because both are commonly misstated. MiCA's stablecoin titles applied from 30 June 2024 — six months before the rest of the regulation, so issuers were in scope before the venues listing them. And the GENIUS Act has two clocks: signed 18 July 2025, it becomes effective on the earlier of 18 January 2027 or 120 days after the primary federal regulators issue final rules, while the prohibition on a digital-asset service provider offering or selling a non-compliant payment stablecoin in the United States bites on 18 July 2028. For exchanges, wallets and distributors, 2028 is the real cliff and 2027 is not. Treasury's implementing proposal was published in August 2026. Regulation and reserve backing do not create an insured bank deposit.
What the market actually looks like

An advisor who cannot size the market cannot assess a proposal about it. Two issuers hold the overwhelming majority of outstanding value, and most of that value moves as trading and collateral rather than as payments — which is the single most useful fact for deflating an overstated stablecoin-payments pitch. Quote a figure with its as-of date and its source, because these move weekly and aggregators disagree.

v: Concentration is the risk that matters to a payments architect. There is no multi-bank scheme here, no shared rulebook and no mutualised default arrangement. Scheme risk and issuer risk are the same risk, and your concentration analysis has one or two names in it rather than forty.

Attestation is not audit. An attestation reports agreed figures at a point in time; an audit opines on the financial statements and the controls behind them. The two market leaders sit at opposite ends of that spectrum, and the difference is worth naming rather than glossing.

The run risk is in the redemption channel, not in the assets. Par redemption is a contractual promise to authorised participants, typically next-day and above a minimum size; everyone else exits into the secondary market at whatever price clears. Short-dated government paper is liquid, but it still has to be sold — which is the fire-sale transmission supervisors worry about. Read each issuer's redemption policy for the minimum size and the cut-off, because that is the number that determines behaviour under stress.

The constraint nobody mentions is elasticity. Additional supply requires full upfront payment, so a stablecoin cannot create intraday credit. A correspondent bank can and routinely does. That is why prefunding costs reappear in any serious corridor design — and it is a structural property of the instrument, not an implementation detail that will be engineered away.

blocks.v: Be careful with volume figures. Most published stablecoin "payment volume" is either company-reported or derived from on-chain activity that includes exchange and treasury movement. Say "reported", give the source, and separate transfer volume from payment volume — the gap between them is usually the whole argument.

See also — place the instrument on the layer model from unit 01.1 before arguing about it: the token is the instrument, the chain is the infrastructure, the issuer's redemption terms are the scheme, and the wallet or exchange is the service. Most claims that stablecoins are faster compare one layer against a rival's four.

blocks.title: Four differences between a tokenised deposit and a stablecoin — have these cold
blocks.v: Liability: a deposit token is a claim on the issuing bank inside the prudential perimeter; a stablecoin is a bearer claim on a segregated reserve pool. Balance sheet: issuing a deposit token is deposit funding, whereas a customer converting deposits into a stablecoin shrinks the bank. Settlement between institutions: at par through existing interbank mechanisms, versus secondary-market price discovery plus authorised-participant redemption. Access: a deposit token travels with the bank's existing customer relationship, so you cannot receive one without being onboarded. The trade is clean — a tokenised deposit removes the run-on-the-reserve mechanic and gives up open access, and open access is the whole reason stablecoins got traction.

J.P. Morgan’s JPM Coin deposit-token proposition is a concrete institutional example. Check current eligibility, networks and permissions; public blockchain infrastructure does not imply unrestricted access or transferability.

Assess EU AI Act duties by intended purpose and role, not by the industry you are in — and then give the actual answer, because the audience needs it. Annex III captures the evaluation of creditworthiness and credit scoring of natural persons, with an explicit exception for systems used to detect financial fraud, plus life and health insurance pricing. Exception triage, address repair, routing, liquidity forecasting and fraud detection are not enumerated, so ordinary payment-operations AI is generally not high-risk. Two consequences: the compliance burden people fear here is largely misattributed, and an agent that begins inferring things about a natural person's creditworthiness has crossed a boundary the same agent doing repair had not. Note also that the stand-alone Annex III obligations were deferred to 2 December 2027 by the 2026 Digital Omnibus. What binds today is not the AI Act: it is DORA, applying since 17 January 2025, together with existing security, privacy, outsourcing and payment obligations — and your model-risk framework.
Model risk is the framework your bank will actually apply

The first question a bank risk officer asks about any payments AI is not "is it high-risk under the AI Act?" It is "who validated it, under what policy, and where is it in the model inventory?" US supervisory guidance on model risk management — SR 11-7 and its equivalents — defines a model as a quantitative method that turns input data into estimates, and requires three things: sound development and implementation, independent validation, and governance with clear ownership. It predates machine learning and does not address it explicitly, which leaves a live ambiguity: is a non-deterministic agent producing a recommendation a model at all? Most institutions are resolving that conservatively by treating it as one, and an advisor who anticipates the question is in a much stronger position than one who is surprised by it.

v: Model inventory. If it is not registered, it does not exist to the second line, and it will be found during an examination rather than before one.
Independent validation. Someone who did not build it tests it against held-out data and against a challenger, and signs off the intended use.
Bounded intended use. The approval is for a stated purpose. Reusing a repair model for a credit decision is a new model, not a new feature.
Ongoing monitoring. Drift in inputs or outcomes, with a defined retraining trigger and a defined behaviour when the model times out or abstains.

Human accountability. The supervisory expectation now stated plainly by the ECB is clear and unambiguous accountability for AI-driven decisions — which in practice means a named owner, not a committee.

blocks.title: The question with no settled answer — have one anyway

It is not an unauthorised transaction, because the authority was real — so the payer-protection route does not obviously open. It is not straightforwardly an authorised push payment scam either, because nobody deceived the customer. It may be a merchant dispute, in which case the card scheme rules apply and the account-to-account equivalent does not exist. Nobody has settled this, and saying so precisely is a stronger answer than pretending otherwise. What you can commit to is the design that keeps the question small: bounded mandates with expiry, per-payee and per-amount limits, revocation that takes effect immediately, and an evidence trail that shows exactly what was delegated and when.

units.title: Answer business and technical challenges
units.objective: Practise concise answers with mechanism, trade-off and evidence boundaries.

blocks.v: Answer directly, explain the mechanism and state the material condition. If a fact is missing, name the source or test that resolves it. Do not substitute a platform feature for a customer outcome.

v.q: Are A2A, instant and RTGS the same?
v.a: No. They describe account endpoints, a service-speed/availability promise and an individual gross-settlement mechanism respectively. One design can combine them without one term implying the others.

v.q: Will pay-by-bank replace cards?
v.a: Fit depends on reach, conversion, protection, credit, recurring use and completed-sale economics. Lower execution fees alone do not determine the merchant or customer choice.

v.q: Why does instant still need liquidity?
v.a: Outgoing settlement can require funds before receipts arrive, including outside funding-market hours. Treasury must fund peak obligations, not merely daily net outflow.

v.q: Can we reroute after a timeout?
v.a: Only after resolving the original safely or following a supported controlled scheme process. Missing evidence is not proof of non-execution; blind rerouting can pay twice.

v.q: Does finality mean no refunds?
v.a: No. Final settlement and a later refund, return, reimbursement or dispute obligation answer different questions. Money can move back without erasing the original settlement.

v.q: Does active-active mean no loss or duplication?
v.a: No. Define ownership, consistency, quorum, durable acknowledgement, fencing and external-effect recovery. Multiple active applications can still use one write primary per shard.

v.q: Does majority acknowledgement guarantee zero loss in every disaster?
v.a: No. Guarantees depend on topology, journaling and assumed failures. Test acknowledged-write survival and disaster recovery; this cannot by itself resolve unknown external settlement.

v.q: How do you obtain exactly-once payments?
v.a: Define the boundary. Atomically bind operation identity to local effects, then use durable attempts, supported duplicate controls, enquiries and reconciliation across networks. Message delivery guarantees alone are insufficient.

v.q: Why MongoDB rather than relational storage?
v.a: Evaluate the workload. Documents can suit rich evolving aggregates and distributed access; correctness requires deliberate transactions, indexes and concerns. Relational designs are also valid. Compare the same controls, cost and operating requirements.

v.q: Does ISO 20022 eliminate mapping?
v.a: No. Versions, profiles and extensions differ. A governed canonical model preserves meaning and provenance; XML-to-JSON conversion alone does not achieve that.

v.q: What does the benchmark prove for this bank?
v.a: It provides measured evidence within the published scope. Use it to design a representative proof with real dependencies, controls, tail latency, failures, accounting outcomes and cost before extrapolating.

v.q: Can AI repair and resend automatically?
v.a: Only under explicit authority, verified data and state-aware controls. It must not invent facts or infer failure from a timeout. Start with evidence assembly and expand bounded actions based on evaluation.

v.q: Are stablecoins always faster and cheaper?
v.a: Compare the entire corridor: acquisition, FX, custody, compliance, transfer, redemption and local payout. Fast token movement is not identical to immediate usable local-currency funds.

v.q: What should we modernise first?
v.a: Start with the measured constraint on the desired service—reach, posting, liquidity, exceptions, control or change cost—and fund an increment with measurable outcomes and a safe migration path.

blocks.v: The 2026 questions — the ones that will come from the floor

The questions above test whether you understand payments. These test whether you have been paying attention this year. Each answer is short on purpose: the credibility comes from the date and the qualification, not from the length.

v.q: Swift moved the structured-address deadline again. What do we do with the programme?
v.a: Keep it running and stop quoting the date. Swift accepted a community request in late August 2026 to extend the migration, so the November 2026 requirement is postponed to a future standards release with revised timing due by December; the EPC held its date pending a September board and has since announced a delay; the Federal Reserve moved its aligned release to November 2027. Unstructured, hybrid and structured all remain valid meanwhile. The destination has not changed and the data-quality work is the long pole, so slowing down now means doing it twice. What changes is the communication: stop presenting a cutover date to the business and start presenting the readiness percentage.

v.q: Is our fraud model high-risk under the EU AI Act?
v.a: Generally no, and the reason is specific rather than general. Annex III captures evaluating the creditworthiness and credit scoring of natural persons, with an explicit exception for systems used to detect financial fraud. Exception triage, address repair, routing and liquidity forecasting are not enumerated either. And the stand-alone Annex III obligations were deferred to 2 December 2027 by the 2026 Digital Omnibus. What binds you today is DORA, applying since January 2025, plus your existing model-risk framework — which is the question your own risk function will ask first anyway.

v.q: Our agent paid the wrong merchant with a valid mandate. Who bears the loss?
v.a: Nobody has settled this, and saying so precisely is stronger than inventing an answer. It is not an unauthorised transaction, because the authority was real, so the payer-protection route does not obviously open. It is not an authorised push payment scam either, because nobody deceived the customer. It may be a merchant dispute, in which case card scheme rules apply and the account-to-account equivalent does not exist. What you can commit to is the design that keeps the exposure small: bounded mandates with an expiry, per-payee and per-amount limits, revocation that takes effect immediately, and an evidence trail showing exactly what was delegated and when.

v.q: Should we issue a stablecoin, hold reserves for someone else's, or do neither?
v.a: Three different businesses with three different risk profiles, and the honest default is the third. Issuing means taking on redemption obligations, reserve management and, in the US, a permitted-issuer regime whose distribution prohibition bites in July 2028 — with the market already concentrated in two names. Holding reserves is a deposit and custody business with concentration and run-correlation risk, and it is the one with a clear revenue line. Doing neither, and instead being reachable for stablecoin on-ramps and off-ramps, captures most of the flow economics with none of the issuance obligations. Ask which of the three the strategy paper is actually proposing, because they usually get conflated.

v.q: Is the digital euro a threat to our deposit base, and by how much?
v.a: The balance-sheet risk looks manageable and the revenue question is genuinely unresolved — and those are different answers to different questions. Holding limits bound the outflow, legal entities cannot hold a balance at all, and the ECB's own modelling puts the stress impact below earlier liquidity stress tests. But no limit has been set; the figure people quote is a hypothetical from financial-stability modelling, not a decision. The sharper commercial issue is that distribution is mandatory, consumer use is free, merchant charges are capped by reference to comparable instruments for a transitional period, and the build is multi-billion across the industry. That is obligation without an obvious revenue line, and the reverse waterfall — real-time access to the funding account at authorisation time — is the expensive part nobody costs properly.

v.q: The US market-structure bill just failed. Does that change our plans?
v.a: For stablecoins, no — they have their own statute and their own dates. For everything else in digital assets, it means the policy question is unresolved rather than settled: cloture failed 49–50 on 15 September 2026, on ethics provisions attached to the bill rather than on the market-structure substance. The practical consequence is that US digital-asset activity beyond payment stablecoins continues to run on agency rulemaking without a statutory foundation, which is a legal-risk position rather than a product position. If a business case depends on that legislation passing, it needs a date-free version.

v.q: You keep saying the benchmark proves resilience. What does it actually prove?
v.a: It proves a bounded thing, and the boundaries are the credible part. The published configuration is twelve application pods, a five-shard event journal and a six-shard operational data store on 32-vCPU shards, in one cloud region across three availability zones. The failure exercise was run at 3,500 payments per second — 58% of peak — so there is no evidence about node loss at 6,000. Primary election averaged about five seconds within that single region, which says nothing about regional loss or cross-region recovery point. And roughly 430,000 database operations per second at 6,000 payments is about seventy-two operations per payment, which is a property of the design rather than a headline throughput number. What remains unreported is write and read concern, the index set and payload shape. Ask for those before extrapolating.

blocks.v: The pattern in every good answer above is the same three moves: state the fact with its date, state the qualification that most people omit, then say what you would actually do. The third move is what distinguishes an advisor from a well-briefed analyst, and it is the one people forget under pressure.

units.title: Frame the Sibos conversation: scale without sacrifice
units.objective: Connect volume, correctness, resilience, data and business value in a clear opening.

v.v: Business obligation. Higher volume matters when customers receive the promised outcome and every obligation remains accounted for.
What scale preserves. Correctness, usable funds, tail latency, liquidity and recovery under peaks, failures and change.
Architectural response. Explicit authority, durable decisions, controlled retries and reconciliation across boundaries.

Evidence and next decision. Give one measured number with its conditions, then convert it into a representative client proof with business outcomes and failure tests. A number without its conditions invites the wrong argument.

blocks.v: Practice opening

Somewhere in this room, a bank paid the same instruction twice this year because a timeout was read as a failure. That is not a capacity problem. It is an authority problem — nobody owned the payment's state at the moment the answer went missing — and it gets worse at four thousand a second, not better. That is what "scale without sacrifice" actually means: the thing you must not sacrifice is knowing, at every instant, who owns each payment and what has been irrevocably decided about it. So the question we should be asking of any architecture is not how many transactions per second it claims. It is four things. Does something own the state of each payment explicitly, or is ownership implied by whichever process happens to be holding it? Are decisions durable before they are acted on, so a retry is safe by construction rather than by convention? Can the platform tell you, during an outage, exactly which obligations are affected — not that it is degraded, but which ones? And is the operational history in a form a machine can actually reason over, because the exception queue is where AI earns its place in payments and it cannot reason over data you threw away at the boundary. We have measured all four, under load and under failure, with Icon Solutions. The numbers are worth discussing, but the conditions are worth more — and the real question is how they translate to your payment mix, your controls and your dependencies.

Prepare three depths: 30 seconds for the recommendation and its condition; two minutes for the flow and the responsibility boundaries; ten minutes for architecture, failure modes and proof. Adapt the emphasis to the audience without changing the underlying facts. And prepare the pivot to the conference's own theme, because you will need it: the reason operational data quality matters now is that it is the input to everything agentic, and an institution that discards structure at the boundary has capped what AI can ever do for its operations. That is a one-sentence bridge from your topic to theirs, and it is better made by you than extracted from you.
