units.title: Glossary of acronyms and payment concepts
units.objective: Resolve any term in this course to a precise definition and to the unit that teaches it, and hold the commonly confused pairs apart under questioning.

blocks.v: Every entry follows concept = definition (Reference - Module XX, Unit YY), so a term you cannot apply to a worked example sends you back to the unit that teaches it rather than to a search engine. Module and unit numbers match the current structure of this course and are checked against it whenever the content is rebuilt.

blocks.title: Use it for the pairs, not just the acronyms
blocks.v: Expanding an acronym is table stakes. What separates an advisor is holding the commonly confused pairs apart under pressure: clearing and settlement; finality and availability; Confirmation of Payee and Verification of Payee; scheme and infrastructure; instrument and service; interchange and merchant service charge; at-least-once delivery and effectively-once processing; the two things called DORA; the two things called PSR; principal risk and liquidity risk; attestation and audit. Each of those is defined separately below, deliberately.

v: 3-D Secure = The card-industry authentication protocol used to shift liability and satisfy strong customer authentication in remote card payments. Its commercial significance is the exemption regime around it, not the protocol. (Reference - Module 01, Unit 07)

blocks.v: A

v: A2A — Account-to-Account = Payment between payment accounts; it does not specify speed, settlement or use of open banking. (Reference - Module 01, Unit 01)
A2A — Agent-to-Agent = Communication between software agents; distinct from account-to-account payments. (Reference - Module 10, Unit 05)

ACH — Automated Clearing House = An electronic credit/debit clearing arrangement, commonly associated with batch processing; exact settlement and return rules depend on the system. (Reference - Module 03, Unit 02)

ACID = Atomicity, Consistency, Isolation and Durability: database transaction properties within a defined boundary, not an atomic guarantee encompassing remote payment settlement. (Reference - Module 08, Unit 02)
ACP — Agentic Commerce Protocol = A specification for programmatic commerce and checkout interactions among buyers, businesses and agents. (Reference - Module 10, Unit 05)
Acquirer = Institution serving the merchant side of card acceptance under applicable contracts, law and network rules. (Reference - Module 01, Unit 07)
Active-active = A deployment in which multiple instances serve work concurrently; write authority, ownership and consistency remain explicit design choices. (Reference - Module 08, Unit 01)

ACWP — Accept Without Posting = FedNow acceptance for specified legal/compliance concerns about beneficiary availability; not a general workaround for slow account posting. (Reference - Module 02, Unit 03)

admi = The ISO 20022 administration message family, covering message rejection and system event notification. Frequently excluded from migration mandates, and frequently forgotten because of it. (Reference - Module 01, Unit 05)

Admission control = Refusing or deferring new work at the edge to protect a saturated system. In instant payments it must reject rather than queue, because a queued payment misses its deadline. (Reference - Module 08, Unit 04)
Agent = Software using tools to pursue a goal; the right to access data or move money must be enforced independently of generated instructions. (Reference - Module 10, Unit 04)
Agentic AI = AI used in goal-directed workflows with tool use and possible actions, ranging from assistance to authorised execution. (Reference - Module 10, Unit 01)
AI — Artificial Intelligence = Methods for prediction, inference, generation or decision support; assess a payment application by its actual purpose and risk. (Reference - Module 10, Unit 01)

AISP — Account Information Service Provider = Provider of account-information services under the relevant permission framework; this access does not itself authorise payment initiation. (Reference - Module 04, Unit 03)
AML — Anti-Money Laundering = Controls against handling criminal proceeds, distinct from but related to fraud and sanctions controls. (Reference - Module 06, Unit 03)
AP2 — Agent Payments Protocol = A protocol for verifiable delegated payment authority through mandates and related credentials; not itself a settlement mechanism. (Reference - Module 10, Unit 05)
API — Application Programming Interface = A defined software interface for exchanging requests and data; a successful call need not prove payment completion. (Reference - Module 04, Unit 03)
APP fraud — Authorised Push Payment fraud = A scam in which a payer is deceived into authorising a payment to a fraudster. (Reference - Module 06, Unit 03)

ART — Asset-Referenced Token = MiCA category for tokens seeking stable value by reference to other values/rights or combinations, rather than meeting the single-currency EMT definition. (Reference - Module 09, Unit 01)
ASPSP — Account Servicing Payment Service Provider = Provider maintaining the relevant payment account and its account-service responsibilities. (Reference - Module 04, Unit 03)
At-least-once delivery = A message is never lost but may be delivered many times. What every durable broker and every retrying client actually provides. (Reference - Module 08, Unit 02)
At-most-once delivery = A message is never delivered twice but may be lost. Acceptable for telemetry, never for a payment. (Reference - Module 08, Unit 02)

Atomicity = The defined changes commit together or none do. Two senses are in play in this course and should not be blurred: the database sense, inside one transaction boundary (Module 08, Unit 02), and the settlement sense, where two legs of an exchange complete together or not at all — delivery-versus-payment and payment-versus-payment (Module 09, Unit 03). (Reference - Module 08, Unit 02)

Attestation versus audit = An attestation reports agreed figures at a point in time; an audit opines on the financial statements and the controls behind them. Know which one you are being shown. (Reference - Module 09, Unit 01)
Authentication = Verification of identity or credentials, distinct from authority to take a specific action and from proof that an action is free of deception. (Reference - Module 04, Unit 03)
Authorisation — card payment = Issuer-side approval under applicable controls, usually before capture, settlement and merchant payout. (Reference - Module 01, Unit 07)
Authorisation — payment authority = Permission to execute the specified action within its scope and applicable legal/contractual rules. (Reference - Module 04, Unit 03)
Availability = Ability to perform a defined service successfully for a stated population and period, with scope and exclusions specified. (Reference - Module 08, Unit 01)

Availability nines = 99.9% permits 8 hours 46 minutes of unavailability a year, 99.99% permits 52 minutes and 99.999% permits 5 minutes 15 seconds. Under a ten-second scheme deadline, missed deadlines matter more than the annual percentage. (Reference - Module 08, Unit 01)
Available balance = Funds presently available to spend after relevant holds, limits and credit rules; can differ from booked balance. (Reference - Module 02, Unit 04)

blocks.v: B

v: B2B — Business-to-Business = Transactions between businesses; also part of the name of the specific SEPA business direct-debit scheme. (Reference - Module 02, Unit 02)

BaaS — Banking as a Service = An arrangement combining regulated banking capabilities and another firm’s proposition, with responsibilities determined by permissions and contracts. (Reference - Module 05, Unit 01)
Back-pressure = Limiting admission or production when downstream work falls behind; protects capacity without extending a payment deadline. (Reference - Module 07, Unit 03)
Bacs = The UK payment system associated with Direct Credit and Direct Debit, rather than a synonym for all account payments. (Reference - Module 03, Unit 01)

BAH — Business Application Header = The ISO 20022 envelope carrying routing, timestamps and the UETR. In FedNow it carries the creation timestamp that starts the timeout clock. (Reference - Module 01, Unit 05)
BASE = Basically available, soft state, eventual consistency — the model usually set against ACID, and the honest description of a read projection. (Reference - Module 08, Unit 02)
Batch / bulk processing = Handling instructions as a group; this alone does not establish whether settlement is gross or net. (Reference - Module 01, Unit 04)
BEN = A beneficiary-borne charges instruction where permitted by the applicable cross-border service; not valid for every scheme. (Reference - Module 03, Unit 04)

Berlin Group = A pan-European standardisation initiative publishing the NextGenPSD2 and openFinance API frameworks. A de facto standard, not a regulator and not a scheme. (Reference - Module 04, Unit 03)
BIC — Business Identifier Code = An ISO-standard organisation identifier commonly used for financial institutions; not a customer account identifier. (Reference - Module 01, Unit 05)
BIS — Bank for International Settlements = International institution supporting central-bank cooperation and hosting work including the CPMI. (Reference - Module 03, Unit 04)
Booked balance = The balance resulting from posted account entries, before considering some holds or other availability restrictions. (Reference - Module 02, Unit 04)
Bridge (cross-chain) = A mechanism moving value representations between chains, introducing custody and validation failure modes that exist on neither chain alone. (Reference - Module 09, Unit 03)
BSON — Binary JSON = MongoDB’s binary document representation with defined data types; still requires modelling and validation decisions. (Reference - Module 07, Unit 02)
Business payment ID = Durable identity linking a logical payment to messages, attempts, ledger entries and cases across its lifecycle. (Reference - Module 07, Unit 02)

blocks.v: C

v: camt = ISO 20022 Cash Management message family, covering defined reporting and investigation functions. (Reference - Module 01, Unit 05)

camt.052 / camt.053 / camt.054 = Bank-to-customer account report, statement and debit/credit notification message types respectively; each has a distinct reporting role. (Reference - Module 01, Unit 05)
camt.056 / camt.029 = Payment-cancellation request and investigation-resolution message types; requesting cancellation does not itself recover settled money. (Reference - Module 01, Unit 05)
Canary release = A controlled deployment to a limited population or workload, evaluated before wider rollout. (Reference - Module 08, Unit 04)
Canonical model = Governed internal representation of payment meaning and lifecycle information, potentially based on ISO 20022 concepts. (Reference - Module 07, Unit 02)
Capture = Submission of an authorised card transaction for financial processing under the applicable timing and amount rules. (Reference - Module 01, Unit 07)
Cardinality (shard key) = The number of distinct shard-key values. Too few caps how far data can spread regardless of how many shards you add. (Reference - Module 08, Unit 03)
CBDC — Central Bank Digital Currency = Digital money that is a direct central-bank liability; retail and wholesale designs differ in users and purpose. (Reference - Module 09, Unit 02)
CBPII — Card-Based Payment Instrument Issuer = A PSD2-context role associated with confirmation of funds, rather than unrestricted account-history access. (Reference - Module 04, Unit 03)

CBPR+ — Cross-Border Payments and Reporting Plus = Swift community usage guidelines for ISO 20022 cross-border messages; a market-practice context rather than a settlement system. (Reference - Module 01, Unit 05)

CDC — Change data capture = Deriving an event stream from a database's change log rather than from application code. An alternative to an application-level outbox, with different ordering and coupling trade-offs. (Reference - Module 07, Unit 03)
CDD — Customer Due Diligence = Identification, verification and risk understanding of a customer relationship, including applicable ongoing measures. (Reference - Module 06, Unit 03)

CDE — Cardholder Data Environment = The systems, people and processes within PCI DSS scope. Segmentation, tokenisation and point-to-point encryption shrink it; none of them eliminate it. (Reference - Module 06, Unit 04)
Central-bank money = A claim on a central bank, distinct from customer deposits that are claims on commercial banks. (Reference - Module 01, Unit 03)
CFO — Chief Financial Officer = Executive responsible for financial management, investment economics and accounting confidence. (Reference - Module 05, Unit 03)
CFPB — Consumer Financial Protection Bureau = US authority associated here with personal financial data rights rulemaking under section 1033. (Reference - Module 04, Unit 04)
CFT — Countering the Financing of Terrorism = Measures against terrorist financing, which can involve lawful as well as unlawful sources of funds. (Reference - Module 06, Unit 03)
Change stream = MongoDB mechanism for observing data changes, requiring consumer checkpoints, duplicate handling and recovery procedures. (Reference - Module 08, Unit 04)
CHAPS — Clearing House Automated Payment System = UK high-value sterling payment system settling through the Bank of England’s RTGS infrastructure. (Reference - Module 03, Unit 01)
Chargeback = A card-scheme dispute process that can create a financial adjustment, distinct from a merchant-initiated refund. (Reference - Module 01, Unit 07)

CHIPS — Clearing House Interbank Payments System = US-dollar payment system combining liquidity-saving mechanisms and continuous intraday finality; not simply end-of-day net settlement. (Reference - Module 03, Unit 02)
Clearing = Exchange/processing of instructions and, where applicable, calculation of payment obligations. (Reference - Module 01, Unit 03)

CLS = The principal payment-versus-payment settlement system for eligible FX currencies and participants. A material share of global FX turnover still settles without PvP protection, which is why this remains a live supervisory topic. (Reference - Module 03, Unit 04)
Command = A request to perform an action or change state, distinct from an event recording that something happened. (Reference - Module 07, Unit 03)
Commercial-bank money = A claim on a commercial bank, such as a deposit; distinguish it from that bank’s central-bank settlement balance. (Reference - Module 01, Unit 03)
Commit point = The point where a defined state change or decision is durable; boundaries across systems can have different commit points. (Reference - Module 07, Unit 01)
Compensation = A new business action intended to offset an earlier one; not necessarily possible or equivalent to rollback of settlement. (Reference - Module 07, Unit 03)

Completed-payment rate = Completed eligible payments divided by eligible attempts, with a stated treatment of retries. The customer-facing measure that technical availability figures tend to flatter. (Reference - Module 11, Unit 01)
Conditional update / compare-and-set = An update allowed only when current state or version matches an expected condition, reducing conflicting concurrent changes. (Reference - Module 08, Unit 02)
Consent / permission = Authority for scoped access/actions, including relevant provider, account, purpose, amount and time constraints. (Reference - Module 04, Unit 03)
Continuous gross settlement = Settlement of individual orders continuously within the operating arrangement, subject to funding and release rules. (Reference - Module 02, Unit 01)
COO — Chief Operating Officer = Executive responsible for service delivery, operations, exceptions and incident recovery. (Reference - Module 05, Unit 03)

CoP — Confirmation of Payee = The UK payee-name checking scheme run by Pay.UK, phased in from 2020 across Faster Payments and CHAPS. Different legal basis, different rails and a different result vocabulary from EU Verification of Payee — the most commonly conflated pair in the domain. (Reference - Module 06, Unit 02)

Correlation ID / causation ID = The identifier linking every event in one business flow, and the identifier of the event that directly caused this one. Together they are what make distributed tracing and dispute reconstruction possible. (Reference - Module 07, Unit 03)
Correspondent banking = One bank providing account/payment services to another, often for currencies or markets it does not access directly. (Reference - Module 03, Unit 04)
Cost per completed payment = Defined relevant costs divided by the specified completed-payment population; distinguish marginal and fully allocated costs. (Reference - Module 11, Unit 01)
Cover payment = The separate funding transfer supporting a customer payment instruction in a correspondent arrangement. (Reference - Module 03, Unit 04)
CPMI — Committee on Payments and Market Infrastructures = BIS-hosted committee working on payment, clearing and settlement analysis and standards. (Reference - Module 03, Unit 04)
CPMI-IOSCO = The CPMI and International Organization of Securities Commissions, joint standard setters behind the PFMI. (Reference - Module 01, Unit 03)
CQRS — Command Query Responsibility Segregation = Separation of change and query models; does not inherently require event sourcing or separate databases. (Reference - Module 07, Unit 03)
Credit transfer = A payer-initiated instruction to transfer funds to a beneficiary under the applicable service rules. (Reference - Module 01, Unit 01)
CRF — Conditional Random Field = A statistical model for structured prediction such as address-component labelling; output is not proof of factual correctness. (Reference - Module 10, Unit 02)
CSM — Clearing and Settlement Mechanism = An arrangement providing clearing and/or settlement services between payment service providers in the relevant context. (Reference - Module 03, Unit 03)
CSM operator = Organisation running a clearing/settlement infrastructure; distinguish it from a body managing scheme rules. (Reference - Module 03, Unit 03)
CTO — Chief Technology Officer = Executive responsible for technology direction, architecture and engineering capability. (Reference - Module 05, Unit 03)

CTPP — Critical ICT third-party provider = A provider designated under DORA as systemically important and brought under direct European oversight. Designation changes the supervisory relationship, not just the contract. (Reference - Module 06, Unit 04)
Cut-off = Latest time an instruction can enter a specified processing or settlement cycle; distinct from the customer’s promised delivery time. (Reference - Module 01, Unit 08)

cVRP — Commercial Variable Recurring Payments = Variable recurring payments used to pay third-party merchants under a commercial scheme with a priced access fee, as distinct from mandated fee-free sweeping between a customer's own accounts. (Reference - Module 04, Unit 04)

blocks.v: D

v: Dead-letter queue = Where messages that cannot be processed are parked for human resolution. Its age profile is an operational metric, not a technical detail. (Reference - Module 08, Unit 04)

Dedupe window = The period over which duplicate operation identities are remembered. Beyond it, a late duplicate becomes a new payment — so the window is a business decision, not a cache setting. (Reference - Module 08, Unit 02)
Deduplication = Recognition and controlled handling of repeated requests/messages, with defined identity, effect and retention scope. (Reference - Module 08, Unit 02)
Deferred net settlement = Settlement of offset obligations at later scheduled times, with exposure managed until settlement becomes final. (Reference - Module 02, Unit 01)

Degraded mode = A pre-agreed reduced service — lower limits, deferred enrichment, a non-instant fallback — permitted under scheme and regulatory rules. The alternative to a binary up or down. (Reference - Module 08, Unit 04)
Deposit token / tokenised deposit = Bank-deposit claim represented using token technology; rights and protection depend on the actual arrangement. (Reference - Module 09, Unit 03)
Direct debit = Payee-initiated collection under a payer mandate, with scheme-specific return, refund and verification rules. (Reference - Module 02, Unit 02)

Direct participation = Participation under an infrastructure’s direct-participant arrangements; technical connectivity and settlement-account ownership remain separate questions. (Reference - Module 01, Unit 04)

DORA — Digital Operational Resilience Act = EU regulation on ICT risk, incident reporting, resilience testing and third-party arrangements for financial entities, applying since 17 January 2025. Not to be confused with the DevOps metric set of the same acronym, below. (Reference - Module 06, Unit 04)

DORA (DevOps Research and Assessment) = The software-delivery metric set — lead time for change, deployment frequency, change failure rate and time to restore service. It shares an acronym with the Digital Operational Resilience Act and means something entirely different; say which one you mean. (Reference - Module 11, Unit 01)
Double-entry bookkeeping = Recording balanced debits and credits in the relevant books; does not imply two institutions share one ledger. (Reference - Module 02, Unit 04)

DPAN = The device or domain primary account number: the token provisioned to a device or merchant in place of the funding PAN, resolvable back to it only by the token service provider. (Reference - Module 04, Unit 01)
Drift = Degradation of model performance as input or outcome distributions move away from training conditions. Requires monitoring and a defined retraining trigger. (Reference - Module 10, Unit 01)
Dual running = Temporary operation of old/new arrangements during migration with one execution owner for each live payment. (Reference - Module 05, Unit 04)

Dual write = Writing to a database and to a message broker as two independent operations with no atomicity between them. The failure mode the transactional outbox exists to remove. (Reference - Module 07, Unit 03)
DvP — Delivery versus Payment = Linking asset delivery to payment to reduce principal risk within defined legal/technical boundaries. (Reference - Module 09, Unit 03)
DvP — Delivery-versus-payment = The securities equivalent: the asset moves only if the cash moves. (Reference - Module 09, Unit 03)
Dynamic QR = A payment code generated for a specific purchase/session, supporting amount and order binding. (Reference - Module 04, Unit 02)

blocks.v: E

v: E-money = Electronically stored value representing a claim on its issuer under the applicable regime, not automatically an insured bank deposit. (Reference - Module 05, Unit 01)
EBA CLEARING = Operator of infrastructures including RT1 and STEP2, distinct from the European Banking Authority regulator. (Reference - Module 03, Unit 01)
ECB — European Central Bank = The central bank at the centre of the Eurosystem, involved in monetary policy and euro payment infrastructure. (Reference - Module 03, Unit 01)
EEA — European Economic Area = The EU Member States plus Iceland, Liechtenstein and Norway; not identical to SEPA geography or the euro area. (Reference - Module 03, Unit 01)

Effectively-once processing = The effect is applied once because the consumer records the message identity atomically with the effect. The property you design for, since exactly-once delivery across a network boundary is not achievable. (Reference - Module 08, Unit 02)

Elasticity (monetary) = The capacity of a monetary system to expand credit to meet settlement needs. A stablecoin requires full upfront payment for any additional supply, so it cannot create intraday credit the way a correspondent bank does — the binding constraint on stablecoin business-to-business settlement. (Reference - Module 09, Unit 01)
Embedding = A numeric vector representation used for similarity search. A search projection, never an authoritative balance or status. (Reference - Module 10, Unit 04)
EMI — Electronic Money Institution = Institution authorised to issue electronic money and provide permitted payment services. (Reference - Module 05, Unit 01)
EMT — E-Money Token = MiCA category for a crypto-asset intended to maintain value by referencing one official currency. (Reference - Module 09, Unit 01)
EMV / EMVCo = EMV originally refers to Europay, Mastercard and Visa; EMVCo maintains payment technology specifications including tokenisation and QR. (Reference - Module 04, Unit 01)
End-to-end ID = Reference intended to follow a payment through the supported customer-to-beneficiary chain; not inherently an enforced duplicate-prevention key. (Reference - Module 01, Unit 05)

Entitlement = The specific rights an identity holds at the moment of action, evaluated at use time rather than at session start. The difference matters the moment an agent runs for hours. (Reference - Module 10, Unit 03)
EPC — European Payments Council = Body managing SEPA payment schemes; not the settlement operator for every SEPA payment. (Reference - Module 03, Unit 01)
EPN — Electronic Payments Network = The Clearing House’s US ACH operator, distinct from CHIPS and RTP. (Reference - Module 03, Unit 02)

Error budget = One minus the service level objective, expressed as permitted failure in a period and spent by both incidents and changes. It converts an argument about whether to ship into an arithmetic question with an agreed answer. (Reference - Module 08, Unit 01)
EU — European Union = Political/legal union whose legislation governs the EU scope discussed here; distinct from SEPA and the euro area. (Reference - Module 03, Unit 01)
Euro area / Eurosystem = Euro area: EU states using the euro. Eurosystem: the ECB plus their national central banks. (Reference - Module 03, Unit 01)
Event = A record of an established fact, such as funds being reserved, rather than a request for it to happen. (Reference - Module 07, Unit 03)
Event sourcing = Use of an authoritative event history to reconstruct aggregate state, with versioning and controlled replay. (Reference - Module 07, Unit 03)
Event-driven architecture = Components react to published events/notifications; the event history need not be the authoritative store. (Reference - Module 07, Unit 03)
Eventual consistency = A model allowing replicas/projections to converge after propagation; lag must not silently replace an authority needing stronger guarantees. (Reference - Module 07, Unit 03)
Evidence register = Record of a claim’s source, date, scope, denominator, calculation and qualifications. (Reference - Module 11, Unit 01)
Exactly-once business effect = One logical operation changes economic state once within a defined boundary; message delivery guarantees alone do not establish it. (Reference - Module 08, Unit 02)
Exception = A condition needing handling outside the normal automated path, with an owner, evidence and permitted next action. (Reference - Module 10, Unit 02)

blocks.v: F

v: Failover = Transfer of a service/data role after failure; payment recovery also requires resolving in-flight work and reconciling outcomes. (Reference - Module 08, Unit 04)
False decline / false positive = A legitimate payment rejected or flagged by controls; assess its cost alongside fraud prevention. (Reference - Module 06, Unit 03)
Faster Payments = The named UK fast-payment service; customer availability and interbank settlement are separate design dimensions. (Reference - Module 03, Unit 01)
FCA — Financial Conduct Authority = UK financial conduct regulator, cited for open-banking and commercial VRP developments. (Reference - Module 04, Unit 04)

FDX — Financial Data Exchange = The US industry body publishing a data-sharing standard, recognised by the CFPB as a standard-setting body under its section 1033 rule. Its standards are not law, and the rule they attach to is currently enjoined. (Reference - Module 04, Unit 04)
FedACH = Federal Reserve ACH service for electronic credits/debits under its operating schedules and rules. (Reference - Module 03, Unit 02)
FedNow = Federal Reserve instant-payment service with defined acceptance, timing, settlement and exception procedures. (Reference - Module 03, Unit 02)
Fedwire Funds Service = Federal Reserve real-time gross settlement funds-transfer service, distinct from FedACH and FedNow. (Reference - Module 03, Unit 02)
Fencing = Preventing a stale/displaced worker from continuing conflicting writes or external actions after ownership changes. (Reference - Module 08, Unit 02)
FI — Financial Institution = Institution providing financial services; appears in ISO names distinguishing interinstitution from customer initiation messages. (Reference - Module 01, Unit 05)
FIDA — Financial Data Access = EU open-finance proposal discussed in the course, with broader scope than payment-account initiation/access. (Reference - Module 06, Unit 04)
Finality = The legally defined point when the relevant settlement is unconditional and irrevocable; later redress obligations may still arise. (Reference - Module 01, Unit 03)
Forward recovery = Completing or repairing outstanding work after a fault when reversing already committed external effects is not possible. (Reference - Module 05, Unit 04)
FSB — Financial Stability Board = International body coordinating financial-stability work, including the G20 cross-border payment agenda. (Reference - Module 03, Unit 04)
Funds availability = When the recipient may use funds, distinct from receipt of a message or some interbank settlement milestones. (Reference - Module 01, Unit 03)
FX — Foreign Exchange = Exchange between currencies, including rate, spread, timing and settlement-risk considerations. (Reference - Module 03, Unit 04)

blocks.v: G

v: G20 — Group of Twenty = International forum sponsoring the cross-border payment improvement agenda referenced in the course. (Reference - Module 03, Unit 04)
Gateway = A controlled connection to processing or infrastructure, with functions depending on the product and context. (Reference - Module 03, Unit 03)
General ledger = An institution’s central accounting record, supported by detailed subledgers and reconciliation. (Reference - Module 02, Unit 04)
Generative AI = Models generating text or other outputs; grounding and validation are still required before consequential action. (Reference - Module 10, Unit 01)

GENIUS Act = US statute for payment stablecoins, signed 18 July 2025. It becomes effective on the earlier of 18 January 2027 or 120 days after final rules; the separate prohibition on offering or selling a non-compliant payment stablecoin in the United States applies from 18 July 2028, which is the operative date for exchanges, wallets and distributors. (Reference - Module 09, Unit 01)

gpi — Global Payments Innovation = Swift's service layer over correspondent banking: a UETR preserved unaltered along the chain, end-to-end tracking, a same-day availability commitment, fee transparency and unaltered remittance data. It made correspondent banking observable; it did not change how it settles. (Reference - Module 03, Unit 04)
Gross settlement = Settlement of each full instruction without offsetting it into a net amount; queues and liquidity coordination can still apply. (Reference - Module 01, Unit 03)
Grounding = Constraining generated output to retrieved, attributable source evidence rather than to the model's own parameters. (Reference - Module 10, Unit 01)
Guardrail = A constraint enforced outside the model, which the model cannot argue past. A rule in a prompt is not a guardrail. (Reference - Module 10, Unit 04)

blocks.v: H

v: Held-out set = Data withheld from training and used to estimate real-world performance. Results quoted without one are not results. (Reference - Module 10, Unit 01)

Holding limit = A cap on individual central bank digital currency balances used as a financial-stability safeguard. No figure has been decided for the digital euro; illustrative amounts used in modelling are not policy. (Reference - Module 09, Unit 02)
Host card emulation = Software-based support for card functionality through the device host environment, with its own credential/security architecture. (Reference - Module 04, Unit 01)
Hot shard = A shard receiving disproportionate traffic because of key skew. Adding shards does not relieve it; changing the key does. (Reference - Module 08, Unit 03)
Hotspot = Concentrated demand or contention on a key, shard or shared resource that limits capacity despite spare resources elsewhere. (Reference - Module 08, Unit 03)
HTTP — Hypertext Transfer Protocol = Web request/response protocol; HTTP 402 is the payment-required status used in x402 interactions. (Reference - Module 10, Unit 05)

Human-in-the-loop = A required human decision inside an automated path, as distinct from after-the-fact review. In payments it is an architectural boundary, not a policy preference. (Reference - Module 10, Unit 02)

blocks.v: I

v: IBAN — International Bank Account Number = Structured account identifier used in participating jurisdictions; valid syntax does not prove payee identity or account status. (Reference - Module 01, Unit 05)

IC++ / interchange-plus = Pricing that passes interchange and scheme fees through at cost with a stated acquirer margin. Transparent, and the card-mix risk sits with the merchant — as against blended pricing, where it sits with the acquirer. (Reference - Module 05, Unit 02)
ICT — Information and Communication Technology = Technology systems/services within the operational-risk scope discussed in DORA. (Reference - Module 06, Unit 04)
ID — Identifier = Value naming an entity or occurrence; payment, instruction, message, attempt and event identities serve different purposes. (Reference - Module 01, Unit 05)
Idempotency = Repeated execution of the same logical request does not repeat its business effect within the defined scope and retention period. (Reference - Module 08, Unit 02)
Idempotency key = Identity for a logical operation, enforced with uniqueness, parameter consistency and durable result/state handling. (Reference - Module 08, Unit 02)

IFR — Interchange Fee Regulation = Regulation (EU) 2015/751, capping consumer debit interchange at 0.2% and consumer credit at 0.3% on EEA intra-regional transactions and imposing business rules. It does not cap scheme fees, commercial cards or the merchant's total acceptance price. The UK mirrors the caps in retained law. (Reference - Module 05, Unit 02)
IMF — International Monetary Fund = International institution publishing research including the historical eNaira adoption case used here. (Reference - Module 09, Unit 04)

In-flight = Work started but not resolved when a boundary changes — a cutover, a failover, a release. Ownership of in-flight items must be explicit, because this is where duplicates and orphans are created. (Reference - Module 11, Unit 04)
Inbound payment = A payment received by the institution whose perspective is being described. (Reference - Module 01, Unit 06)
Inbox / idempotent consumer = Pattern recording processed message identity atomically with its local effect to make repeated delivery safe. (Reference - Module 07, Unit 03)
Indirect participation / sponsor = Access through another participant, with defined settlement, funding, service and dependency arrangements. (Reference - Module 01, Unit 04)

Instant / real-time payment = Rapid recipient availability under a named service’s rules, commonly with continuous availability; exact timing/finality is system-specific. (Reference - Module 01, Unit 01)
Instruction ID = Reference for a payment instruction in a specified relationship/context, distinct from its message envelope or transmission attempt. (Reference - Module 01, Unit 05)

Intent Mandate / Cart Mandate / Payment Mandate = The three mandate types in the AP2 agent payments specification: a delegation made when the human is not present and carrying an expiry; a human-present authorisation bound to specific items and payee; and a signal of agent presence and transaction modality to the network and issuer. (Reference - Module 10, Unit 05)
Interchange = A fee between card-side institutions under applicable rules, typically from acquiring to issuing side; caps and exemptions vary. (Reference - Module 01, Unit 07)
Interoperability = Systems working together across format, meaning, participation, settlement and legal/commercial layers. (Reference - Module 04, Unit 02)

Intraday credit = Central-bank or sponsor credit extended within the operating day to bridge settlement timing. Generally unavailable outside operating hours, which is what makes weekend instant-payment funding a treasury problem. (Reference - Module 02, Unit 01)
IPF — Icon Payments Framework = Icon Solutions’ framework for building/configuring payment capability; assess the exact modules, integrations and deployment. (Reference - Module 07, Unit 04)
IPR — Instant Payments Regulation = EU Regulation 2024/886 amending euro credit-transfer rules, with obligations differentiated by provider and geography. (Reference - Module 06, Unit 02)
ISO / ISO 20022 = International Organization for Standardization / its financial business-model and messaging standard, broader than one syntax. (Reference - Module 01, Unit 05)

ISO 8583 = The long-standing card message standard still carrying most authorisation traffic, distinct from ISO 20022 and migrating slowly. Running both is the normal state, not a transitional one. (Reference - Module 01, Unit 07)
Isolation = Rules governing concurrent transaction visibility and conflicts; specify the actual guarantee rather than assuming all transactions are serialised. (Reference - Module 08, Unit 02)
Issuer = Institution serving the cardholder side and issuing the credential, with authorisation and other duties under the arrangement. (Reference - Module 01, Unit 07)

blocks.v: J

v: JPM Coin = J.P. Morgan institutional deposit-token proposition used as a specific case; current access and transfer conditions require verification. (Reference - Module 09, Unit 03)
JSON — JavaScript Object Notation = Text data-interchange syntax common in APIs; conversion to JSON does not itself preserve semantics or meet an XML profile. (Reference - Module 07, Unit 02)

blocks.v: K

v: KYB — Know Your Business = Due diligence on a business customer, including applicable legal identity, ownership and risk information. (Reference - Module 06, Unit 03)
KYC — Know Your Customer = Customer identification/verification within the broader due-diligence framework, not a substitute for ongoing controls. (Reference - Module 06, Unit 03)

blocks.v: L

v: Latency = Elapsed time between defined events, reported with workload and percentile rather than an unqualified average. (Reference - Module 08, Unit 01)
Least privilege = Only the access/actions needed for a task, with explicit scope, expiry and revocation. (Reference - Module 10, Unit 04)
Ledger = Authoritative accounting record for a defined scope; orchestration state and analytics are not automatically ledgers. (Reference - Module 02, Unit 04)
Legal tender = An obligation to accept an instrument in discharge of a debt. Proposed for the digital euro, and a core driver of its acceptance economics. (Reference - Module 09, Unit 02)
LEI — Legal Entity Identifier = Standardised legal-entity identifier; identifies a different object from an account number or payment reference. (Reference - Module 01, Unit 05)
Linearizable read = A read with a real-time consistency guarantee under documented database constraints, stronger than merely reading committed data. (Reference - Module 08, Unit 02)
Liquidity = Funds or reliably available funding to meet obligations when due; expected receipts are not necessarily present settlement funds. (Reference - Module 02, Unit 04)

Liquidity efficiency = Value settled per unit of funding resource over a stated time profile. The measure that makes a settlement-design argument commercial rather than architectural. (Reference - Module 11, Unit 01)
Liquidity-saving mechanism = Coordinated release or offset of eligible obligations to reduce funding needs under a system’s rules. (Reference - Module 02, Unit 01)
LLM — Large Language Model = A generative model trained on language and other representations; fluent output does not prove truth or authorisation. (Reference - Module 10, Unit 01)
Lossy mapping = Transformation unable to transmit all source meaning, requiring preservation and an approved treatment of lost detail. (Reference - Module 07, Unit 02)

blocks.v: M

v: Majority read concern = MongoDB read guarantee concerning majority-committed data; not automatically the freshest value. (Reference - Module 08, Unit 02)
Majority write concern = Acknowledgement according to majority durability conditions; guarantees depend on topology, journaling and failure assumptions. (Reference - Module 08, Unit 02)
Mandate — agent payment = Evidence of delegated checkout/payment authority with constraints such as beneficiary, amount, purpose and expiry. (Reference - Module 10, Unit 05)
Mandate — direct debit = Payer authority for collections under a named scheme, with scope, evidence and lifecycle requirements. (Reference - Module 02, Unit 02)

MCP — Model Context Protocol = A standard for exposing tools and data to models, increasingly the transport layer beneath agent deployments. Its security properties are the deployment's security properties. (Reference - Module 10, Unit 04)
Merchant of record (MoR) = Legal seller for the transaction, carrying sale, tax and customer duties under the applicable arrangement. (Reference - Module 05, Unit 01)
Message ID = Identity of a message instance/envelope, not necessarily a unique economic payment. (Reference - Module 01, Unit 05)

MiCA / MiCAR — Markets in Crypto-Assets Regulation = EU regime for crypto-assets and their service providers. The stablecoin titles covering asset-referenced and e-money tokens applied from 30 June 2024; the remaining titles from 30 December 2024 — it is not a single start date. (Reference - Module 09, Unit 01)
ML — Machine Learning = Statistical learning from data, used for scoring, forecasting and anomaly detection with purpose-specific evaluation. (Reference - Module 10, Unit 01)

Model inventory = The register of models in use, their owners, intended uses and validation status. If a model is not in it, it does not exist to the second line of defence — and it will be found during an examination rather than before one. (Reference - Module 10, Unit 04)

Monetary sovereignty = A state's control over the money used in its economy. Since 2024 it has done more to sustain central bank digital currency programmes than the financial-inclusion argument ever did. (Reference - Module 09, Unit 04)
Monotonic key = A steadily increasing shard-key value, such as a timestamp or sequence, which sends all new writes to one shard. The classic cause of a hot shard. (Reference - Module 08, Unit 03)

MPM / CPM = EMVCo's merchant-presented and consumer-presented QR modes. Merchant-presented needs no merchant hardware and dominates globally; consumer-presented is used where the merchant must control the moment, such as a transit gate. (Reference - Module 04, Unit 02)

MSC / MDR — Merchant Service Charge / Merchant Discount Rate = The all-in price an acquirer charges a merchant per card transaction: interchange plus scheme fees plus acquirer margin. The only card number a merchant's CFO actually sees. (Reference - Module 05, Unit 02)
MT — Message Type = Swift traditional message notation; migration obligations vary by message/service rather than one universal disappearance date. (Reference - Module 06, Unit 01)

Mule account = An account, often opened by a real person who has been recruited or coerced, used to receive and move on criminal proceeds. The reason a Verification of Payee match proves identity rather than honesty. (Reference - Module 06, Unit 03)

blocks.v: N

v: Nacha = Organisation governing US ACH Network rules, distinct from operators such as FedACH and EPN. (Reference - Module 03, Unit 02)

Net debit cap = The maximum net obligation a participant is permitted to reach in a deferred net system; the cap is the control and the prefunded account is the evidence for it. (Reference - Module 02, Unit 01)
Net settlement = Settlement of obligations after offsetting eligible amounts, under defined exposure and default arrangements. (Reference - Module 01, Unit 03)

NII — Net interest income = Income from the spread between the return on assets funded by payment-related balances and the cost of those balances. The deposit-side economics of a payments franchise, and what instant execution actually changes. (Reference - Module 05, Unit 02)
Nostro / vostro = Our account with another bank / another bank’s account with us, viewed from our institution’s perspective. (Reference - Module 03, Unit 04)
Notional pooling = Combining eligible balances for interest calculation without necessarily physically transferring them; legal/liquidity treatment varies. (Reference - Module 10, Unit 03)

blocks.v: O

v: OCT Inst — One-Leg Out Instant Credit Transfer = EPC scheme governing the qualifying euro leg of payments with a leg outside SEPA, not identical rules for every global leg. (Reference - Module 02, Unit 02)

ODA — Offline data authentication = Terminal-side cryptographic verification of a card's authenticity without going online, in static, dynamic and combined forms. The mechanism behind transit gates that must decide in well under a second. (Reference - Module 04, Unit 02)

ODFI / RDFI = Originating and Receiving Depository Financial Institution in the US ACH network. The ODFI introduces an entry and warrants its authorisation; the RDFI posts it to the receiver's account. (Reference - Module 03, Unit 02)
ODL — Operational Data Layer = Architecture making operational information available across systems with defined authority, freshness and governance. (Reference - Module 08, Unit 05)
ODS — Operational Data Store = Store supporting operational queries/context, potentially combining sources; it is not automatically authoritative for every decision. (Reference - Module 08, Unit 05)
Offline payment = A payment with some party/system disconnected; distinguish credential authentication, deferred submission and offline value transfer. (Reference - Module 04, Unit 02)
On-ramp / off-ramp = The conversion points between bank money and tokens. Off-ramp access, not chain speed, usually determines whether a corridor is actually usable. (Reference - Module 09, Unit 03)
On-us payment = Transfer within one institution’s books, potentially avoiding external settlement but still requiring controls and accounting. (Reference - Module 01, Unit 06)
Open banking = Controlled account-data access and/or payment initiation under authorised arrangements; not itself a settlement rail. (Reference - Module 04, Unit 03)
Open finance = Controlled access to financial data beyond traditional payment-account scope, with jurisdiction-specific frameworks. (Reference - Module 06, Unit 04)
Orchestration = Coordination of payment tasks, decisions, deadlines and integrations with explicit state/recovery rules. (Reference - Module 07, Unit 01)
OUR = Payer-borne charges instruction under an applicable cross-border arrangement, subject to scheme rules. (Reference - Module 03, Unit 04)
Outbound payment = A payment sent by the institution whose perspective is being described. (Reference - Module 01, Unit 06)
Outbox = Publication intent committed atomically with a local business change, with relay retries and consumer deduplication still required. (Reference - Module 07, Unit 03)
Outcome unknown = Insufficient authoritative evidence to establish execution or failure, requiring controlled enquiries and reconciliation. (Reference - Module 01, Unit 02)
Overlay = An interface or added service above underlying payment arrangements, such as aliases or a wallet journey. (Reference - Module 04, Unit 01)

blocks.v: P

v: P2P — Person-to-Person = A use case involving individuals, not a particular instrument or settlement network. (Reference - Module 03, Unit 02)
p50 / p95 / p99 = Latency values at or below which 50%, 95% or 99% of observations fall for the defined population. (Reference - Module 08, Unit 01)
pacs = ISO 20022 Payments Clearing and Settlement message family for interinstitution functions. (Reference - Module 01, Unit 05)
pacs.002 / pacs.004 = Payment-status report / payment-return message types; a status report is not a returned value movement. (Reference - Module 01, Unit 05)
pacs.008 / pacs.009 = FI-to-FI customer credit transfer / financial-institution credit transfer message types, constrained by versions and profiles. (Reference - Module 01, Unit 05)
pain = ISO 20022 Payments Initiation message family, commonly used at customer-to-bank boundaries. (Reference - Module 01, Unit 05)
pain.001 / pain.008 = Customer credit-transfer initiation / customer direct-debit initiation message types, subject to supported profiles. (Reference - Module 01, Unit 05)
PAN — Primary Account Number = The card-account number used in card processing, subject to applicable security and data-handling controls. (Reference - Module 04, Unit 01)
PAR — Payment Account Reference = A reference linking eligible card credentials/tokens; not an authorisation credential or universal customer identity. (Reference - Module 04, Unit 01)
Partition — network failure = A communications failure separating parts of a distributed system, distinct from deliberate partitioning for scale. (Reference - Module 08, Unit 01)
Partition / shard = A subset of data/workload distributed across resources; distinguish database placement from application work ownership. (Reference - Module 08, Unit 03)
Pay-by-bank = A merchant proposition using bank-account payments, often open-banking initiated; not one universal scheme or protection model. (Reference - Module 04, Unit 04)

Pay.UK = Operator and standards body for Faster Payments, Bacs and the Image Clearing System. It sets the rules and runs the schemes; it is not the Bank of England and it is not the infrastructure provider. (Reference - Module 03, Unit 01)
Payee / beneficiary / recipient / creditor = Related receiving-side terms whose exact legal/message roles depend on context. (Reference - Module 01, Unit 06)
Payer / debtor / sender / remitter = Related paying-side terms; distinguish the party owing/paying funds from any agent initiating on its behalf. (Reference - Module 01, Unit 06)
PayFac — Payment Facilitator = Provider supporting sub-merchant acceptance under an acquiring arrangement with delegated onboarding, risk and servicing duties. (Reference - Module 05, Unit 01)
Payment aggregate = A bounded group of payment state/data with explicit identity and consistency rules, not an unlimited container for every history record. (Reference - Module 07, Unit 01)
Payment hub = Platform coordinating payment execution/controls across channels and infrastructures with defined account, risk and treasury integrations. (Reference - Module 07, Unit 01)
Payout = Transfer to a merchant, seller or recipient, possibly later than the original purchase’s settlement. (Reference - Module 01, Unit 07)

PCI DSS — Payment Card Industry Data Security Standard = Security standard for relevant card-data environments; tokenisation can affect scope without automatically removing all duties. (Reference - Module 06, Unit 04)

Peg = The reference value a stablecoin targets and the mechanism sustaining it. A peg is an objective, not a contractual guarantee; the contractual guarantee, if any, is the redemption right. (Reference - Module 09, Unit 01)

PEP — Politically Exposed Person = A person entrusted with a prominent public function, together with their relatives and close associates, attracting enhanced due diligence. (Reference - Module 06, Unit 03)

PFMI — Principles for Financial Market Infrastructures = CPMI-IOSCO standards addressing infrastructure risks including liquidity, finality and operations; direct applicability depends on scope. (Reference - Module 01, Unit 03)
PI — Payment Institution = Institution authorised for specified payment services under the relevant regime, not automatically a deposit-taking bank. (Reference - Module 05, Unit 01)

PISP — Payment Initiation Service Provider = Provider initiating a payment order at another PSP at the user’s request without holding payer funds as part of that service. (Reference - Module 04, Unit 03)
Pix = Brazil’s instant-payment arrangement, distinct from a retail CBDC claim. (Reference - Module 09, Unit 04)
POBO / COBO = Payments on Behalf Of / Collections on Behalf Of: centralised treasury execution preserving underlying parties and legal authority. (Reference - Module 10, Unit 03)

Positive and negative confirmation = The SCT Inst messages by which the beneficiary's PSP states that funds were made available or that the transaction was rejected. They are what the 5, 7 and 9-second boundaries are measured against. (Reference - Module 02, Unit 03)
Posting = Recording an account entry; specify how it relates to settlement and usable funds. (Reference - Module 02, Unit 03)

Pre-validation = Checking beneficiary account details and the destination jurisdiction's payment rules before a cross-border payment is sent. Its value is a network effect, so coverage rather than capability is the constraint. (Reference - Module 03, Unit 04)
Prefunding = Placing eligible funds before settlement obligations arise under the system’s arrangements. (Reference - Module 02, Unit 01)

Principal risk (Herstatt risk) = The risk that one party delivers and the other fails before delivering back. Named after the 1974 Bankhaus Herstatt failure, and the reason payment-versus-payment settlement exists. (Reference - Module 02, Unit 01)

Programmable payment versus programmable money = Conditional execution of a payment instruction, versus conditions embedded in the money itself. Only the second constrains what the holder can subsequently do, which is why the distinction is politically as well as technically significant. (Reference - Module 09, Unit 03)

Project Nexus = A BIS-originated blueprint for multilateral interlinking of domestic instant-payment systems, now carried forward by Nexus Global Payments, a legal entity established in 2025 by six Asian central banks. Not live. (Reference - Module 03, Unit 04)
Projection / materialised view = Derived read model built from authoritative changes/events; can lag and needs controlled rebuild and access rules. (Reference - Module 07, Unit 03)
Prompt injection = Instructions embedded in untrusted content attempting to redirect an AI system beyond its intended task or authority. (Reference - Module 10, Unit 04)
Provenance = Evidence of data origin, time and transformations, supporting verification, investigation and audit. (Reference - Module 07, Unit 02)
PSD2 / PSD3 = Second / proposed third EU Payment Services Directive; distinguish current duties from reform milestones and future application. (Reference - Module 06, Unit 04)
PSP — Payment Service Provider = Entity providing payment services within its legal/contractual framework, potentially a bank or eligible non-bank. (Reference - Module 05, Unit 01)
PSR — Payment Services Regulation = Proposed EU regulation accompanying PSD3 reform, distinct from an already applicable requirement. (Reference - Module 06, Unit 04)
PSR — Payment Systems Regulator = UK regulator referenced for APP reimbursement; different meaning from the EU legislative acronym. (Reference - Module 06, Unit 03)
Push / pull payment = Payer-initiated transfer / payee-initiated collection under authority; rights follow the instrument and scheme. (Reference - Module 02, Unit 02)
PvP — Payment versus Payment = Linking final transfer of one currency to final transfer of another to reduce FX principal risk within scope. (Reference - Module 09, Unit 03)
PvP — Payment-versus-payment = Settlement in which the two currency legs of an FX transaction complete together or not at all, eliminating principal risk. (Reference - Module 02, Unit 01)

blocks.v: Q

v: QR — Quick Response code = Machine-readable data carrier; scanning it does not itself prove payee authenticity or settlement. (Reference - Module 04, Unit 02)
Quorum = The required subset of distributed participants for a decision or acknowledgement, whose guarantees depend on topology and failures. (Reference - Module 08, Unit 01)

blocks.v: R

v: RAG — Retrieval-augmented generation = Retrieving authorised source records at inference time so output can be attributed to evidence. Retrieval must carry the same permission filters as the tools, or it becomes a data-leak path. (Reference - Module 10, Unit 04)
Rail = Informal shorthand for a payment system/network/route; clarify scheme, access, clearing and settlement components. (Reference - Module 01, Unit 01)
Read concern = MongoDB’s selectable read consistency/isolation behaviour, chosen with the required session, transaction and write guarantees. (Reference - Module 08, Unit 02)
Recall / cancellation request = Request to stop or recover a payment under applicable rules, not proof that money was recovered. (Reference - Module 01, Unit 02)
Reconciliation = Comparison of independent payment, settlement and accounting records followed by resolution of differences. (Reference - Module 02, Unit 04)
Redemption = Exchange of an issuer claim/token for the promised money under its terms, distinct from a secondary-market sale. (Reference - Module 09, Unit 01)
Refund = A later payment/adjustment returning money under applicable rules, distinct from original settlement finality and card disputes. (Reference - Module 01, Unit 07)

Register of information = The DORA inventory of ICT third-party arrangements that a financial entity must maintain and submit. The first artefact a supervisor asks for, and the one most institutions underestimate. (Reference - Module 06, Unit 04)
Regulation II = US Federal Reserve regulation addressing scoped debit interchange and routing, with exemptions. (Reference - Module 01, Unit 07)
Release gate = A defined evidence condition that must be satisfied before a change is rolled out more widely. A date is not a gate. (Reference - Module 11, Unit 04)
Remittance information = Data explaining commercial purpose, such as invoice references, used to match payments to obligations. (Reference - Module 07, Unit 02)
Replay = Reprocessing historical events to rebuild state or test logic, with external side effects disabled or safely controlled. (Reference - Module 07, Unit 03)
Replication / replica set = Maintenance of copies for availability/durability; serves a different purpose from sharding data for capacity. (Reference - Module 08, Unit 03)
Request to Pay = Messaging requesting a payer to act/respond; the request is not the separate underlying payment. (Reference - Module 02, Unit 02)
Reservation / hold = Restriction on available funds pending later action, with defined release, expiry and posting rules. (Reference - Module 02, Unit 04)

Reserve assets = The assets an issuer holds against outstanding tokens. Quality, custody, segregation and liquidity determine what happens under redemption stress — and the run risk sits in the redemption channel, not in the assets. (Reference - Module 09, Unit 01)

Restoration = The originator PSP's obligation, where no confirmation arrives in time, to lift the reservation and return the payer's account to its prior state. A prescribed remedy, not evidence that the external transfer never happened. (Reference - Module 02, Unit 03)

Resume token = The checkpoint marking a consumer's position in a change stream. If the underlying change history has aged out, the token is unusable and a controlled rebuild is required. (Reference - Module 08, Unit 04)

Retry storm = Correlated client retries after a recovery, which can re-saturate the service that has just come back. The reason recovery plans need rate limits as well as restarts. (Reference - Module 08, Unit 04)
Return = A value movement back under applicable payment rules, linked to rather than erasing the original settlement. (Reference - Module 01, Unit 02)

Reverse waterfall = The mechanism by which a payment exceeding a digital euro wallet balance automatically draws the shortfall from the user's linked commercial bank account at the moment of payment. It is what makes a holding limit workable, and the hardest item on a distributor's build list. (Reference - Module 09, Unit 02)
Revocation = Withdrawal of future authority under defined timing, not necessarily reversal of already irrevocable execution. (Reference - Module 10, Unit 05)

RfP — Request for Payment = The request message on the US RTP network. Distinct from SEPA Request-to-Pay and from the generic concept; the acronyms are close and the schemes are not. (Reference - Module 03, Unit 02)
Routing = Selection of an eligible execution path with safe treatment of existing attempts and constraints. (Reference - Module 01, Unit 08)
RPO — Recovery Point Objective = Target maximum data-loss window for a defined failure/recovery scenario; an objective is not proof of achievement. (Reference - Module 08, Unit 01)
RT1 = EBA CLEARING’s euro instant-payment system with defined participant positions and settlement/access arrangements. (Reference - Module 03, Unit 01)
RTGS — Real-Time Gross Settlement = Individual real-time settlement without amount netting; does not itself imply retail or continuous weekend access. (Reference - Module 01, Unit 01)
RTO — Recovery Time Objective = Target time to restore a defined service after disruption, beyond merely restarting a process. (Reference - Module 08, Unit 01)
RTP network = The Clearing House’s US instant-payment network, distinct from Request to Pay and generic real-time-payment terminology. (Reference - Module 03, Unit 02)
Runway (liquidity) = Time remaining before a funding resource is exhausted at the current rate of use. The number an instant-payments treasury desk actually watches. (Reference - Module 11, Unit 04)

blocks.v: S

v: Safeguarding = Protection/separation of relevant customer funds under payment/e-money rules, distinct from bank deposit insurance. (Reference - Module 05, Unit 01)
Saga = Coordination of local transactions and possible business compensations without a single global rollback. (Reference - Module 07, Unit 03)
Same Day ACH = Nacha's expedited ACH option, with three daily windows and a per-transaction limit of $1m. Eligibility and return rights differ from standard ACH. (Reference - Module 03, Unit 02)
Sanctions controls = Measures applying relevant restrictions to persons, entities or transactions, with scope distinct from AML and fraud. (Reference - Module 06, Unit 03)
SCA — Strong Customer Authentication = Authentication under required independent-factor rules, not proof that a payment is free of deception. (Reference - Module 04, Unit 03)
Scatter-gather = A query issued without the shard key, broadcast to every shard and merged. Correct, and it does not scale. (Reference - Module 08, Unit 03)
Schema / implementation profile = Data structure / additional version-specific business constraints imposed by a scheme or market practice. (Reference - Module 07, Unit 02)
Scheme / scheme manager = Payment rules and standards / the body managing them, distinct from running a specific infrastructure. (Reference - Module 01, Unit 01)

Scheme fee = Fees charged by a card network to issuers and acquirers for authorisation, clearing, settlement, licensing and data. Uncapped by the IFR and the fastest-growing component of the merchant service charge since the caps came in. (Reference - Module 05, Unit 02)
SCT — SEPA Credit Transfer = EPC standard euro credit-transfer scheme with rules distinct from SCT Inst. (Reference - Module 03, Unit 01)
SCT Inst — SEPA Instant Credit Transfer = EPC instant euro transfer scheme defining specific execution, timing and exception requirements. (Reference - Module 03, Unit 01)
SDD Core / SDD B2B = SEPA Direct Debit Core / Business-to-Business schemes, with differing eligibility and refund/control requirements. (Reference - Module 02, Unit 02)

SEC code = The Standard Entry Class code identifying an ACH entry's authorisation type and channel — for example PPD, CCD, WEB and TEL. It determines the applicable warranties and return rights. (Reference - Module 03, Unit 02)
Secure element = Protected hardware environment for credentials and cryptographic operations in supported payment designs. (Reference - Module 04, Unit 01)
SEPA — Single Euro Payments Area = Framework/geography for harmonised euro payments, extending beyond the euro area; not one infrastructure. (Reference - Module 03, Unit 01)
Settlement = Discharge of payment obligations using an agreed settlement asset under the relevant rules. (Reference - Module 01, Unit 03)
Settlement asset = The claim transferred to discharge an obligation, such as central-bank or commercial-bank money. (Reference - Module 01, Unit 03)

Settlement Finality Directive = EU (and retained UK) law protecting transfer orders entered into a designated system from being unwound by a participant's insolvency. It is why "final" is a legal statement about a named, designated system rather than a description of a message having arrived. (Reference - Module 02, Unit 01)
SHA = Shared-charges instruction under an applicable service, subject to scheme-specific charging rules. (Reference - Module 03, Unit 04)
Shadow processing = Copied/replayed work used for comparison while preventing duplicate live payment execution. (Reference - Module 05, Unit 04)
Shard key = Fields determining document distribution; cardinality, skew and query patterns affect scalability and targeting. (Reference - Module 08, Unit 03)
Sharding = Horizontal distribution of data across resources; does not remove hot keys or coordination costs. (Reference - Module 08, Unit 03)

Sibos = Swift's annual financial-services conference. Sibos 2026 runs 28 September to 1 October 2026 in Miami, under the theme of digital finance for AI-driven economies — which is why the AI and digital-money material in this course is stage-relevant rather than optional. (Reference - Module 11, Unit 03)

Singleness of money = The property that every form of money in a system exchanges at par with every other. One of the three tests the BIS applies to a monetary arrangement, alongside elasticity and integrity, and the one stablecoins most visibly fail. (Reference - Module 09, Unit 01)
SLA — Service-Level Agreement = Contractual commitment with defined scope/measurement, distinct from a legal deadline or internal objective. (Reference - Module 02, Unit 03)

SLI — Service level indicator = The specific measurement a service is judged on, such as the ratio of successful eligible attempts. Distinct from the objective set for it and from any contractual commitment. (Reference - Module 08, Unit 01)
SLO — Service-Level Objective = Measurable service target used to guide engineering and operations, such as deadline success or tail latency. (Reference - Module 08, Unit 01)
Smart contract = Programmed logic executed on a ledger/platform; execution alone does not establish legal rights or eliminate external risk. (Reference - Module 09, Unit 03)
Snapshot — event-sourced state = Recorded aggregate state at a known event position to accelerate reconstruction, with later events still required. (Reference - Module 07, Unit 03)
Snapshot read concern = MongoDB point-in-time read semantics under documented deployment/transaction constraints. (Reference - Module 08, Unit 02)

SQL — Structured Query Language = Language used to define and query relational data; database scalability and correctness depend on implementation and workload, not the language label alone. (Reference - Module 08, Unit 05)

SR 11-7 / model risk management = The US supervisory framework requiring sound model development, independent validation and clear governance. It predates machine learning and does not address it explicitly, leaving a live question about whether a non-deterministic agent producing a recommendation is a model — most institutions are answering yes. (Reference - Module 10, Unit 04)
SRTP — SEPA Request-to-Pay = EPC messaging scheme for requests/responses, with payment execution through a separate service. (Reference - Module 02, Unit 02)

Stablecoin = Crypto-asset designed to track a reference value, whose stability and redemption rights depend entirely on the issuer, the reserve and the mechanism. Place it on the course layers before arguing about it: the token is the instrument, the chain is the infrastructure, the issuer's redemption terms are the scheme, and the wallet or exchange is the service. (Reference - Module 09, Unit 01)
Standing order = Payer instruction for scheduled recurring transfers, distinct from a payee-initiated direct debit. (Reference - Module 02, Unit 02)
Static QR = Reusable payment code, often requiring separate amount/reference input or confirmation. (Reference - Module 04, Unit 02)

STEP2 / STEP2-T = EBA CLEARING SEPA infrastructure whose current continuous gross settlement design differs from its superseded net-cycle model; STEP2-T is the service label appearing in the operator resource. (Reference - Module 03, Unit 01)
STP — Straight-Through Processing = Completion without defined manual intervention; specify denominator and treatment of downstream exceptions. (Reference - Module 11, Unit 01)

STR / SAR = Suspicious Transaction Report or Suspicious Activity Report: the filing made to a financial intelligence unit when suspicion of money laundering or terrorist financing arises. The output of AML monitoring, and the clearest reason AML is not fraud prevention. (Reference - Module 06, Unit 03)
Strangler approach = Progressive migration of selected functions/flows around an existing system with explicit routing and retirement. (Reference - Module 05, Unit 04)
Subledger = Detailed accounting for a domain, reconciled to the general ledger and external evidence. (Reference - Module 02, Unit 04)
Swift = Society for Worldwide Interbank Financial Telecommunication and its messaging services, distinct from settlement-account arrangements. (Reference - Module 03, Unit 04)

blocks.v: T

v: T2 = The Eurosystem RTGS service within TARGET services, distinct from TIPS and customer instant schemes. (Reference - Module 03, Unit 01)
Tail latency = Slow-end latency, often p95/p99, revealing delays concealed by averages. (Reference - Module 08, Unit 01)
TARGET = Trans-European Automated Real-time Gross settlement Express Transfer; specify the particular TARGET service when discussing mechanics. (Reference - Module 03, Unit 01)
Target / zero balancing = Physical transfers moving account balances to a target or zero, with funding, timing and accounting duties. (Reference - Module 10, Unit 03)

Targeted financial restrictive measures = The EU's formal term for sanctions applying to named persons and entities. Under the Instant Payments Regulation, PSPs verify their own customers against these lists at least daily and immediately on a new designation, rather than screening each euro-area instant payment. (Reference - Module 06, Unit 02)
TCO — Total Cost of Ownership = Relevant acquisition, integration, operation, change, migration and exit costs over the solution’s lifecycle. (Reference - Module 05, Unit 02)
Throughput = Completed work per unit time under stated conditions; distinguish payments, messages and database operations. (Reference - Module 08, Unit 01)

Time-Out Deadline = The 7-second point in SCT Inst by which the beneficiary PSP's CSM must hold a confirmation, failing which it generates a negative confirmation itself. (Reference - Module 02, Unit 03)
Timeout = Expiry of a waiting/processing interval, not by itself proof that an external action failed. (Reference - Module 01, Unit 02)
TIPS — TARGET Instant Payment Settlement = Eurosystem instant settlement service in central-bank money, distinct from SCT Inst scheme governance. (Reference - Module 03, Unit 01)
TLPT — Threat-led penetration testing = DORA's advanced testing regime for significant entities, conducted against live production systems on a multi-year cycle. (Reference - Module 06, Unit 04)

Token domain restriction controls = The EMVCo controls binding a payment token to a presentment mode, a device and sometimes a merchant. These, rather than the randomness of the token value, are what make a stolen token close to worthless. (Reference - Module 04, Unit 01)

Token requestor = An entity — wallet provider, merchant or PSP — registered with a token service provider to request tokens for a defined use domain, carrying identification and verification obligations. (Reference - Module 04, Unit 01)
Tokenisation — credential = Replacement of sensitive payment credentials with controlled-use tokens and supporting lifecycle/security mechanisms. (Reference - Module 04, Unit 01)
Tokenisation — financial asset = Representation of a financial claim using token technology, without automatically changing issuer or legal rights. (Reference - Module 09, Unit 03)

Tokenised deposit = A commercial bank deposit represented on a ledger. It is a liability of the issuing bank inside the prudential perimeter, transferable only between onboarded parties, and settles at par through existing interbank mechanisms — which is what distinguishes it from a stablecoin. (Reference - Module 09, Unit 03)

Tool call = The permission-checked interface through which an agent takes an action. The enforcement point for authority — which is why read and write must be separated here rather than in the prompt. (Reference - Module 10, Unit 02)
TPP — Third-Party Provider = Umbrella term for relevant account-access providers; verify service scope, permissions and jurisdiction. (Reference - Module 04, Unit 03)
TPS — Transactions per Second = Throughput measure whose transaction must be defined; payment TPS differs from database-operation rate. (Reference - Module 08, Unit 06)
Transaction — database = Defined database operations under selected atomicity, isolation and durability semantics, distinct from the complete economic payment. (Reference - Module 08, Unit 02)
TSP — Token Service Provider = Provider of payment-token provisioning/lifecycle services in the relevant tokenisation framework. (Reference - Module 04, Unit 01)

Two-phase commit = A coordinator-driven atomic commit across participants. Unavailable across institutional boundaries in payments, which is why sagas and compensation exist instead. (Reference - Module 07, Unit 03)

blocks.v: U

v: UETR — Unique End-to-End Transaction Reference = Standardised tracking reference used in relevant Swift flows, not a replacement for all duplicate controls. (Reference - Module 01, Unit 05)
UK — United Kingdom = Jurisdiction of the UK arrangements discussed, with a currency and legal framework distinct from the euro area. (Reference - Module 03, Unit 01)
Unique index = Constraint preventing duplicate indexed values within supported scope; sharded collections impose specific key requirements. (Reference - Module 08, Unit 03)

Unwind risk = The risk that a failed participant's transactions are removed from a deferred net cycle and every other participant's net position is recalculated. Prefunding and finality rules exist to prevent it. (Reference - Module 02, Unit 01)
UPI — Unified Payments Interface = India’s account-payment interface/ecosystem, distinct from Account Aggregator data sharing and retail CBDCs. (Reference - Module 09, Unit 04)
URL — Uniform Resource Locator = Address of a web resource; payment QR codes can contain URLs whose resolved content/destination must be verified. (Reference - Module 04, Unit 02)
US — United States = Jurisdiction containing the distinct FedACH, Fedwire, FedNow, CHIPS and RTP arrangements discussed. (Reference - Module 03, Unit 02)

blocks.v: V

v: Virtual account = Identifier or subledger arrangement improving allocation/reconciliation; determine whether it is a separate legal bank account. (Reference - Module 10, Unit 03)

Vocalink = The Mastercard-owned provider of the central infrastructure behind Faster Payments and Bacs, under contract to Pay.UK. Distinguishing operator from infrastructure provider is the point of naming it. (Reference - Module 03, Unit 01)
VoP — Verification of Payee = Checking supplied payee name against the account identifier before authorisation, returning defined match/unavailability outcomes. (Reference - Module 06, Unit 02)
VRP — Variable Recurring Payments = Recurring bank-payment initiation under defined authority and limits, with different commercial and sweeping arrangements. (Reference - Module 02, Unit 02)

blocks.v: W

v: Wallet = Interface that may store credentials, hold value or initiate payments; identify the underlying liability and funding source. (Reference - Module 04, Unit 01)

Waterfall / reverse waterfall = Proposed digital-euro links moving excess receipts to a bank account or obtaining account funding for payment, subject to final design. (Reference - Module 09, Unit 02)

Wholesale CBDC = A central-bank liability restricted to eligible financial institutions for interbank or securities settlement, distinct from a retail CBDC available to the public. (Reference - Module 09, Unit 04)
Working set = The data and indexes actively in use, which should fit in memory. The real determinant of whether a given shard count is sufficient. (Reference - Module 08, Unit 03)
Write concern = MongoDB write acknowledgement/durability policy; timeout does not prove that a write did not happen. (Reference - Module 08, Unit 02)

blocks.v: X

v: x402 = Protocol for HTTP payment-required interactions with supported verification/settlement mechanisms, not a universal protection regime. (Reference - Module 10, Unit 05)
XML — Extensible Markup Language = Structured syntax used by many ISO 20022 profiles; validity requires applicable schema and business constraints. (Reference - Module 07, Unit 02)

blocks.v: Z

v: Zone sharding = Placement of key ranges on designated shard groups; residency also requires review of copies, backups, logs and access. (Reference - Module 08, Unit 03)

blocks.title: Read the primary sources, and read them in this order

The order that works: the rulebook or legal text for what is required, the operator's page for how it is actually implemented, the supervisor's page for status and dates, and analysis last, for interpretation. If you quote a date on a stage, it should have come from the first three.
